title: Fat Tuesday
logline: Lundi Gras and Mardi Gras: a king arrives by river, an old friend waits on the levee, the whole house wears paper bags with eyeholes, somebody else turns nineteen — and at midnight the horses come down Bourbon Street, and it’s Lent.

s01.slug: MONDAY · 6:40 AM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE ATTIC
body: The gable window comes up gray around the box fan. It stands dead in the frame where somebody set it last summer and left it. The light gets through the blades in bars and lies along the three mattresses and the boards in between. Over Jack’s face the roofing nails come down through the deck in their rows, dry this morning, and Remy’s Tiger poster has let go of a corner in the night and hangs over him at a slant, Tiger in Sunday red with his fist up, celebrating something on a green Jack can’t see. The attic keeps the night’s cold till noon, like his father’s garage in February.

Two houses down, behind a shut window, a radio has a man on WWL doing the Lundi Gras forecast for anybody up at this hour: cold today, cold on the river tonight for the king, and for tomorrow, folks, dig out the long johns.

Jack kneels on the boards at the window and says the penance from memory, the eleventh morning of it. It comes out word-perfect from the summoning to the oil, with *take nothing for the journey* falling in the middle where it always falls, and when it’s done he gets up with the grain of the boards printed on both knees.
The RAZR is on the sill. The outside screen says two, both from Burnaby, both from while he slept.

body.text: wrapped. the violets rode home in my lap like a baby
dutch says good morning to new orleans. dutch has never said good morning to anyone
wrapped. read your book in the van. the guy who had it before you underlined all the wrong parts
dutch says good morning to new orleans. dutch has never said good morning to anyone

He can see the van: the heater blowing, the rest of the crew asleep against the windows with their hoods up, and Skye in the middle seat with the white violets held level on her knees through every turn, the way you’d hold a baby that had finally gone down.
body.else: He can see the van: the heater blowing, the rest of the crew asleep against the windows with their hoods up, and Skye in the middle seat with a used Flannery O’Connor open on her knees, arguing in the margins with a stranger’s pencil.

body: And Dutch. Dutch, who flies the moon on a crane over Burnaby all night and has never in his life said good morning to anyone, has said it to New Orleans on her say-so. Jack stands at the window in his socks and laughs at that without making a sound, so as not to wake the attic, and answers short, with his thumb, so she can read it with one eye open.

body.text: sleep. tell the violets goodnight for me
sleep. fight the pencil guy tomorrow

body: He shuts the phone and drops it in the Carhartt where it hangs on its nail by the window.

By the hatch, Kevin is awake. He lies on his back on top of his sleeping bag, dressed down to his shoes, turning his Bold over and over on his chest, so that the screen lights his chin from below and goes dark and lights it again.
“Bà Nội,” he says, when he sees Jack see it. “Voicemail. She left it at midnight her time. She couldn’t wait for the rosary.”

He puts it to his ear again. From across the attic Jack can hear it play, small and quick and dry, an old woman’s Vietnamese with the rosary’s rhythm still in it, and Kevin lies listening with his eyes shut until it stops.
In the middle Theo is a long shape under a Marisol blanket with his back to the room, asleep, or giving the role everything he has.

body.text: “Happy birthday,” Jack says.
body.else: Kevin says it to the nails over his sleeping bag: “It’s my birthday. Respectfully. Don’t.”

body.text: Kevin turns the phone face-down on his chest. “Respectfully. Don’t.”

body: He turns his head on the pillow to say the rest of it to Jack. “It’s a Monday. Mondays are red beans. Nobody needs a cake on a Monday.”

choices.key: On Lundi Gras morning Kevin told you not to make anything of his nineteenth birthday. You told him you were telling Celeste.
response: “That’s a betrayal,” Kevin says.
“It’s Monday. It’s a small one.”
Kevin takes his own pulse at the wrist, out of habit. “…Lemon,” he says. “If she asks.” Under the boards a lid goes down on a pot, and somebody turns the fire up beneath it.

choices.key: On Lundi Gras morning Kevin told you not to make anything of his nineteenth birthday. You told him you were telling Laney.
response: “She decreed *nothing*,” Kevin says.
“For her. She didn’t decree anything for you.”

Kevin sits up on his sleeping bag and looks at Jack across Theo with new respect. “You’re a dangerous man, Costigan.” At the foot of the stairs Mémère has started in on somebody in French — the beans, or the hour, or both — and the house is getting up under her.

choices.key: On Lundi Gras morning Kevin told you not to make anything of his nineteenth birthday. You told him it would stay between the two of you.
response: “Ours.” Kevin tries the word out with the phone flat on his chest. “Okay. Ours.”
Up through the hatch comes the smell of the red beans Celeste put on at six, and under it her whisper on the stairs, giving the twins their orders.

s02.slug: MONDAY · 7:05 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — RED BEANS
body: Celeste’s 13-inch sits on the end of the counter by the bread box with the sound down low. On WWL a man in a purple tie stands in front of the parishes doing the Lundi Gras forecast — gray, cold, *bundle up for the king* — while the closings crawl along under his shoes: the post office, the banks, the federal building, everything with a flagpole, for Presidents’ Day.

Monday is red beans. The pot went on at six in the dark, a ham bone and a pound of pickled pork and the beans that soaked all night in the yellow bowl, and it has hours to go yet and the rest of the day after that to get better. Mémère sits on a kitchen chair at the stove’s elbow in her housecoat, with her beads, watching it. That is her job, all of it, and she does it like a lifeguard: she does not take her eyes off the water.

Celeste is in navy scrubs with her Touro badge clipped at the pocket, packing her lunch at the counter like a med cart: thermos, apple, napkin, the sandwich last, everything where her hand will expect to find it at one o’clock. She works Lundi Gras, seven to three. Mardi Gras is a different story.

“Mardi Gras she’s had off since nineteen ninety-eight,” Tony tells the kitchen from his chair at the end of the table, over his coffee, proud as if he’d won it off a man in a card game. “Twelve years. Never once gave it back.”

Jack comes to the counter for a mug, and Celeste hands him the roll of wax paper instead, and he holds it while she tears. With her back to the kitchen and her eyes on the sandwich, she says, just above a whisper:

body.text: “Miss Dot tells me violets. The girl in Canada. Did she like the violets?”
body.else: “Lena says you sent a book. The girl in Canada. Did she like the book?”

body: “Yes ma’am.”
“Good.” A fold of wax paper. “And she knows where you are.”
“Yes ma’am. She told me to come.”
Celeste takes that in for the length of a second fold, corner over corner, creased down with her thumbnail.
“Hm.”
She puts the sandwich in the bag on top of the apple.

body.text: At a quarter past she has her keys off the nail and the lunch bag over her wrist, and at the back door, while she checks her badge, Jack leans down to her ear. *It’s Kevin’s birthday.*
Celeste’s face does nothing at all. She looks at the clock over the stove, and at the pantry door, and at the clock again.
“Lemons,” she says, and goes.
At a quarter past she kisses Tony on the top of his head, takes her keys off the nail, and goes out the back with the lunch bag over her wrist.

Laney comes down a minute later, following the smell of the coffee, in a terrycloth robe with a towel wound round her head like a turban, and Jack meets her at the bottom of the stairs. “It’s Kevin’s birthday.”
“Since *when*?”
“Since nineteen years ago.”
She turns on the step without a word and goes back up at a run, the coffee forgotten, the turban coming loose over one ear.

body: At twenty past, Lena comes down in the Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt with the crab on the front washed nearly pink, her hair still wet at the ends, and his black Bic behind her ear. She pours two cups of chicory at the stove. His she does first, with the milk in it, without asking how, and sets it down at his elbow on her way past; then she pours her own.
Not a soul at the table remarks on it. Mémère, at her post by the pot, takes her eyes off the beans long enough to see it, and puts them back.

The twins have the far end of the table. Josie has the *Times-Picayune*’s parade map spread out over her cereal and is going over Zulu’s route in yellow highlighter, and Jude eats around her elbow without complaint.

Remy comes down the stairs on the backs of his heels with a blanket round his shoulders and points at Jack from the doorway. “Ohio owes a king cake. It’s been three days. In some parishes that’s a felony.”

Tony gets up and takes his market jacket off the hook — green canvas, BROUSSARD’S over the heart in white thread, the cuffs gone stiff with ice — and zips it to his chin. Mr. Alcide opened the store at six. Broussard’s takes the Mardi Gras orders Monday morning, six to noon, and after that the door stays shut through Fat Tuesday. “Wednesday I open at six,” Tony says. He finds his keys in the jacket pocket and looks across the kitchen at Jack.

body.text: “You know ice.”
body.else: “You can lift.”

body: “He owes Remy a king cake,” Lena says from the stove in the same second, the coffeepot still in her hand.

Theo sits at the table with chicory and no phone. His phone has been zipped into Kevin’s windbreaker for a week, and he holds the cup in both hands for something to hold. “Choose wisely,” he says. “One of those is a woman and one of them is a refrigerator.”
“They’re both errands,” Kevin says, and butters his toast.

response: Tony’s keys are already in the air, coming at him end over end across the kitchen, and Jack takes them against his chest. “You drive,” Tony says, and takes a piece of Kevin’s toast for the road.

s03k.slug: MONDAY · 10:20 AM · A BAKERY ON CARROLLTON AVENUE — AND BACK ALONG THE STREETCAR LINE
s03k.music: The Meters — “They All Asked for You”
body: The bakery smells of butter and yeast and cinnamon and the burnt-sugar edge of whatever came out of the ovens at four, and the line runs out the door and past the next storefront, where it stamps its feet on the sidewalk and blows on its hands.
Josie is the chaperone. This was Josie’s own idea, announced at the foot of the stairs with her coat already buttoned, and no one in the kitchen came up with a reason fast enough to stop her.

body.text: She wears the king’s medallion on over her school sweatshirt on a holiday, the beads doubled so it rides high where the line can see it.
The king’s medallion rides on Lena’s jean jacket, its beads looped twice round a button, and Josie has looked at it more than once.
The king’s medallion went to Laney on Saturday, and Josie, who has nothing round her neck but a scarf, has mentioned this.

body: She keeps score of everything. They aren’t through the door before she announces, to her sister, “That’s two times you looked at him.”

Inside, the radio behind the register is on WWOZ, and the line is a parade that hasn’t started yet. Lena narrates it for him in her float voice, the one she uses from the top of a ladder, turned down to half for indoors. She knows every order in it. Here, on your left, Sister Bernadette with a list for the convent, four plain and two praline and one cream cheese she will tell you is for Father. Behind her a cop off the night shift, still in uniform, who has earned a whole cake and is going to eat it in his car. And by the door a man in a Zulu warrior’s grass skirt over long johns and a Saints parka, buying four — “That’s Mr. Batiste’s nephew,” Lena tells Jack, low and proud. “He walks tomorrow. He needs his strength.”

body.title: Chalkboard over the register
body.text:
KING CAKES
PLAIN · CINNAMON · CREAM CHEESE · PRALINE · APPLE
NO HALVES · DON’T ASK
THE BABY IS INSIDE · CHEW WITH CARE

body: At the counter Josie says, “Cream cheese.”
“Plain,” Lena says.
“Cream cheese is *better*.”

Lena turns to her sister with the gravity of Thomas opening an article. “It would seem that a king cake ought to be cream cheese, because cream cheese is better. On the contrary, it is written on that chalkboard: *plain*. I answer that a king cake is a *bread*, Josephine Broussard, it is a bread for the Epiphany, it is a bread the Magi would recognize if they walked through that door this minute, and the Magi had never heard of Philadelphia.”
“The Magi never had a king cake at *all*.”
“Which is why they kept walking.”

The cop off the night shift snorts. The counter girl, who is maybe sixteen and has been on her feet since five, reaches into the case for a plain one, and turns it to slide it in a box, and there on the bottom of it, poking out through the dough, is a small pink plastic foot.
“No ma’am,” Lena says. “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian, look at it, the foot is *out*. That baby is pre-located. Where’s the sport in that? Open us a fresh one, please, cher, from the back.”
The girl looks at her, and at the line, and goes to the back for a fresh one. Jack pays, in twenties folded small from the back of his wallet, and that is the debt.
“That’s *three*,” Josie says.
“I was looking at the *change*.”
The counter girl tapes the box shut and slides it across. “You know the rule,” Lena tells Jack, as he picks it up. “You get the baby, you buy the next one.”
“I know the rule.”
“You know it like a man who read it on a placemat. In this city it is *binding*.”
Out on the sidewalk Jack says, “You did a disputation. On a pastry.”
“I did a disputation on *tradition*, Youngstown. The pastry was the occasion.”
“Josie had a point about the Magi.”
“Josie had a point about cream cheese, and the point is she likes it. That is not a point. That is an appetite.”
“I’m *right here*,” Josie says.

It’s colder on Carrollton than it was going in. A red streetcar goes up the neutral ground with its bell going and nobody on it but the motorman. They walk back along the tracks toward Mid-City, Josie a step ahead, the box under Jack’s arm, and every porch they pass is getting ready for tomorrow: ladders chained to the rails with their seat-boxes painted in somebody’s colors, a woman on a stepladder hanging a papier-mâché jester from her porch light, a yard flying a fleur-de-lis and a Saints flag and a Bud Light banner, all three, and on one shotgun still waiting on its repairs, the old spray-paint from the Storm faded orange on the siding by the door, under a string of beads. At the curb at Bienville, waiting on a pickup with purple streamers on its antenna, Lena says:

“The Lundi Gras I was nine, Rex waved at me from the boat. Right at me. I could see his eyes. I decided right there I was going to marry him.” The pickup goes by. “He was sixty-two. I’d have made it work.”

She doesn’t look at him to tell it. Jack says, “Sixty-two,” and can’t find anything to put after it. Josie, a step ahead, has heard every word, and he watches her put it away behind her eyes for later.

Lena has no gloves, and her hands are pulled up inside her sleeves. Jack shifts the box to his left arm. With his right hand he takes hold of the edge of the Carhartt’s pocket and holds it open, and keeps walking. It is a small thing to do with a coat pocket. He knows exactly what it is.

Her hand comes out of her sleeve and goes into the pocket with his. She keeps her eyes on the streetcar tracks while it happens, as if her hand were some other girl’s business. Her fingers are cold. His close over them in the dark of the pocket, among the lint and a folded church bulletin from Thursday, and he can feel each one of them separately, the knuckles, the ridge of a callus where she holds a pen, and he wants the walk to be longer than it is, and he knows exactly how much he wants it. Higher up, in the breast pocket, the RAZR rides with Dutch’s good morning in it, beside her tin.
At the next corner Josie stops and turns round to face them, walking backward.
“Are y’all *going* together? Because Destiny Thibodeaux’s sister says if he carries the box it counts.”
“*Josie.*”
“I’m asking for *science*.” She has been sitting next to Margot on the piano bench all weekend, and it shows.

choices.text: *Carry the box. Let her keep her hand where it is.*
response: He carries the box. Twelve blocks, under the live oaks along the neutral ground and then the bare crape myrtles of the side streets, and her hand doesn’t move in his pocket for any of them. Josie walks ahead of them backward most of the way, watching, and trips on a root heaving up the sidewalk, and keeps watching.

At the gate on Dupre Street Lena takes her hand back to work the latch. In the kitchen Remy is still in his blanket at the table, and she sets the box down on the oilcloth in front of him. “Don’t say I never.”
“I’m *telling* her,” Josie says.
“You will not,” says Lena.

They argue it the rest of the way home, every block of it, Josie walking backward and Lena walking forward, and Lena’s hand stays in his pocket through every point she makes. In the kitchen Remy has the lid of the box up before it’s all the way down on the oilcloth. “Don’t say I never,” Lena tells him, and shuts it on his fingers.

He holds the box out to Josie. She takes it in both arms, outraged — she is a chaperone, not a porter — and carries it home in front of her, level and stiff, like a crown on a cushion. Lena’s hand stays in his pocket anyway.
On Dupre Street Josie marches it into the kitchen and puts it down on the oilcloth with a bang. Lena reaches past her and turns the box round so the bakery’s name faces Remy. “Don’t say I never.”

s03t.slug: MONDAY · 9:00 AM → 12:10 PM · BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD, BANKS STREET — THE WALK-IN
s03t.music: The Meters — “They All Asked for You”
body: By nine the bell over Broussard’s door has stopped ringing separately and become one long jangle, and the line goes out past the window onto Banks Street, everybody in it in a coat and half of them in purple. Tomorrow half of Mid-City boils, and half of Mid-City is buying from Tony: red mesh sacks of crawfish, alive and clicking, going out the door on shoulders and in the beds of trucks and once, at twenty past nine, in a baby stroller.

Jack is the one bringing them out of the walk-in. In past the heavy steel door, a sack off the stack and onto his shoulder, out through the plastic strips, down the length of the case to the counter, and back. By ten he has the rhythm of it, sack, shoulder, door, counter, the kind of dumb good rhythm Frank used to say was the only part of the plant he missed.
Under the front window Mr. Alcide opens oysters for the Monday trade and sings along in French with whatever WWOZ gives him on the red radio, whether or not it was in French to begin with.

Lena has the register and the book. She has the wall phone on its cord tucked against her shoulder and her own LG open on the counter on speaker and a man in front of her with cash in his hand — three customers — and she is taking all three at once and writing it down on a roll of butcher paper with his black Bic: *DUPLANTIS 2 SX 4:00 · MRS. VO 1 SX + 2 DZ · FIREHOUSE 3 SX — CALL BACK, THEY ALWAYS CHANGE IT*. “Ask Lena,” Tony says all morning, to everybody, about everything, and goes on weighing.

Her voice carries the length of the store over the radio and the bell and the crawfish, and every time Jack comes out through the plastic strips it is the first thing that reaches him, before the warm does. *Mrs. Vo, I have you down for four o’clock and if you come at three-thirty I will be at the rosary.* *No sir, those are the small ones, you want the select, I would not lie to you during Carnival.* Tony defers to her on the book the way he defers to the weather.
Once, coming back past the register, Jack has the Bic pointed at him.
“The firehouse changed it.”
“To what?”

“To four. They always change it. Four sacks, and one of them is for Father Hébert, and you do not say that in front of Mrs. Vo or she will want one for Father too.” The pen goes back behind her ear. She has the wall phone off the hook on its first ring, and he goes back into the walk-in with four in his head.
At half past ten Miss Earline comes in, in her plastic rain bonnet, for a pound and the news. She looks down the case at Jack with a sack on his shoulder.
“They haven’t sent you home yet,” Miss Earline says.
“No ma’am.”
“Good. Don’t let them.” She takes her shrimp and gives Lena the news — whose ladder is where on St. Charles, whose roof is leaking, which of the Duplantis girls is expecting — and goes.
At a quarter to eleven Tony follows him into the walk-in and pulls the door shut behind them.

It’s a small room, steel to the ceiling, with one bulb in a wire cage and the compressor droning somewhere over their heads. The sacks are stacked chest-high along the back wall, and in the mesh the crawfish move against each other with a sound like rain starting on a tin roof. Their words smoke when they talk. For a minute they don’t; they stack, Tony handing down and Jack laying the sacks in rows on the pallet by the door, for the afternoon pickups.

“Wednesday,” Tony says, to the sacks, “every Catholic in this city remembers he’s supposed to eat fish. Forty days. I’ll sell more catfish by Easter than I sold all of Advent.” He hands down another sack. “Lent’s been good to me. You won’t hear a word against it from me.”
He doesn’t hand down the next one. “So which one of you is with who?”
Jack stops with a sack in his arms.

Tony lays it out on his fingers, thick fingers, an old knife scar white across one knuckle. “You and her. Her and the singer. You and Canada.” Three fingers, standing up in the bulb light. He looks at them himself. “I’m asking because Celeste says don’t ask, and I been not asking since Tuesday, and I’m done.”
Jack stands in the walk-in with forty pounds of live crawfish against his chest and opens his mouth, and there is nothing in it. *I’m with Skye* is true. It’s the first finger he can’t get past.
Tony waits. The compressor cuts out overhead, and the room is quiet except for the crawfish, and Tony waits through that too, looking at Jack with his three fingers still up.
“That’s what I figured,” he says.

He picks up a sack. He puts his shoulder to the steel door and opens it on the warm and the radio and his daughter’s voice saying *four o’clock, Mrs. Vo, and not one minute before*, and goes out into it.

Jack stays where he is a minute, in the steel room with the bulb and the crawfish, the sack still against his chest. When he carries it out through the plastic strips into the warm, Lena, writing, holds her hand out sideways for a ticket. When nothing lands in it she looks up and sees it’s him, and the hand goes back to the butcher paper.

At a quarter to twelve Clovis leans on his horn out on Banks Street. Lena takes her jacket off the hook, tells her father the book balances to the penny and the firehouse will call back, and tells Jack, on her way past the case, “Don’t let him charge you interest.”
At noon Tony walks down to the bakery by the bank and comes back with a white box, and hands it to Jack across the counter.
“Your debt,” Tony says. “I fronted it. You owe me.”
Then he takes a piece of shirt cardboard from under the register, and a roll of tape, and goes to the door, and turns the sign, and tapes the cardboard up inside the glass under it.

body.title: Hand-lettered, taped inside the door at Broussard’s
body.text:
CLOSED · MARDI GRAS
OPEN ASH WEDNESDAY 6 A.M.
GOD WILLING

body: He presses the tape down at the corners with his thumb, one corner at a time, his back to the store.

response: He says it to Tony’s back. Tony doesn’t turn round. He runs his thumb along the last strip of tape. “Then you’re the only honest man in my store.”

When the truck pulls up on Dupre Street at half past twelve, Lena is on the porch swing between the twins with her feet up on the rail, and she looks at the white box, and at her father, and at Jack, and whatever was said in the walk-in she leaves where it was said.

choices.text: *Carry the king cake home on your lap in the truck.*
response: He carries it out to the truck in both hands and gets in with it, and holds it on his knees all the way back, one hand on the lid and one underneath, over every pothole between Banks Street and Dupre, and the road from one to the other is mostly pothole. Tony drives and watches him do it and says nothing, which on Tony is a sentence.
“Ohio,” Tony says, pressing down the last corner, “you *are* my tab.”
He is still laughing at it at the red light on Broad, and still at it when he pulls up on Dupre Street, with the box on Jack’s knees and the radio off.

s04.slug: MONDAY · 4:45 PM · SPANISH PLAZA, THE RIVERFRONT — LUNDI GRAS
body: The river is higher than Jack thought a river could get and still stay in its banks, and browner, and faster. It goes by the foot of Canal Street without a sound, heavy and steady and not stopping for anybody, like the line at Lordstown when Frank was on it.

Tony has taken whoever is home down to the river on Lundi Gras to watch the king come in since Luc was two. Today that is Clovis, who drove the truck, and Remy, and the twins, and Theo and Laney and Margot and Kevin, and Lena, and Jack. Mémère stayed with the beans.

body.text: Celeste, home at half past three with her badge still on and a paper sack of lemons, stayed with Mémère. “Somebody has to be here,” she said at the door, “when a king comes back from the river.”
body.else: Celeste, home at half past three with her badge still on, stayed with Mémère. “Somebody has to be here,” she said at the door, “when a king comes back from the river.”

body: Spanish Plaza is a round of colored tile at the foot of Poydras with a fountain in the middle and the Riverwalk at its back, and by a quarter to five it is full: purple and green and gold over parkas, children up on shoulders, old men in folding chairs brought from home, a brass band at the far side of the fountain playing for itself and anybody else. Upriver the lights along the big bridge are coming on. A towboat shoves six barges up against the current, slow as a man pushing a stalled car uphill, and the Algiers ferry crosses in front of everything with its own lights on, going home.
“Zulu came in by water already,” Remy announces, with authority. “The king. On a boat. Up there somewhere.” He waves at the river in general. “I missed it.”
Kevin has his hands in the pockets of his windbreaker and is explaining to Jude how a towboat steers when it’s pushing instead of pulling. Jude listens to every word of it.

Lena has Margot by the sleeve at the rail and is giving her the lore without coming up for air: the boat, the king on the deck, the mayor on the landing, *Daddy says the mayor hands him the key and the king gives the city back to us for a day*, and why a king needs a boat at all — “because the city’s a port, Margot, *everything* important comes up that river, including Daddy’s shrimp and the Spanish.”
Margot looks at the river through her black frames. “So the monarchy arrives by freight.”
“*Exactly.*”

“Picture it,” Theo says at Jack’s shoulder, his hands deep in the pockets of the good coat. “A king. A boat. A city that hands him the keys and asks for nothing back but beads. Costigan, it’s *Fitzcarraldo* with a horn section.”

body.text: Tony comes along the rail with a go-cup of coffee and stops behind them, Lena at the rail and Jack beside her, and puts his arm out between them, level, like the gate at a railroad crossing.
body.else: Tony has his spot at the rail behind the twins. He had his say in the walk-in this morning. He looks at the two of them now, Lena at the rail and Jack beside her, over Josie’s head, just the once.

body.text: “So which one of you is with who?”
“*Daddy.*”
“I’m *asking*. A man can ask on a public levee.”

There is no answer from either one of them. The boat’s horn gives one instead, far off down the river around the bend where nobody can see it yet, a long low note that comes up the water and turns every head on the plaza, and Tony takes his arm back and goes to look.
body.else: Far off down the river, around the bend where nobody can see it yet, a boat’s horn sounds, one long low note coming up the water, and every head on the plaza turns.

body: The rail fills two deep behind the sound. There’s room at it for Lena and not much else. Jack could step back to the fountain with Theo. He puts his arms on the rail instead, one on either side of her, his hands on the cold iron beside hers, and stands at her back with the plaza behind him. Saturday on Orleans Avenue she was the one behind.

He doesn’t touch her anywhere he doesn’t have to. He keeps a little cold air between his chest and her back and keeps it there on purpose, and it costs him, and he could name the price item by item standing here: the back of her neck where her hair is pinned up off it, right under his chin; the red beans and Celeste’s shampoo. After a minute she leans back into him. He lets her.
“You’re blocking the wind, Youngstown,” she says, without turning round.
“That’s the idea.”
“Good idea.”

She stays. Out on the water the ferry has turned for the Algiers side, and downriver the light is going out of the sky a shade at a time, and across the fountain the brass band has slowed into something with a long horn in it.

The wind comes up the river and moves her hair against his chin. His arms are round a space he isn’t going to close. He keeps his hands on the cold iron for the next ten minutes, and it is the hardest work he has done all day.

Wes is at the edge of the plaza by the floodwall, where the crowd thins out against the concrete: the bent brim, a go-cup, the same two friends from Gentilly in their Saints jackets. He is thinner than he was on Canal Street a week ago, or the coat is bigger. He sees Lena before she sees him. When she does, she ducks out under Jack’s arm and goes to him through the crowd, and Wes opens his arms, and she walks into them.
“You’re skinny,” she tells him, into his coat.
“You look like your mama.”
“I do *not*.”
“Every day more, dawlin’.”
Lena lets go first. Wes holds on a second longer than she does, and then he is the one who steps back. She brings him to the rail by the sleeve of his coat.
“Ohio,” Wes says.
“Wes.”

Then the twins arrive at Lena’s elbows, Josie wanting to see the king’s face and Jude wanting to see the engine, and she takes one in each hand and steers them down through the crowd toward the front rail on the water. Wes stands where she was, beside Jack, with his forearms on the iron and the go-cup between his hands, looking at the river.
“Y’all staying for the king?” Wes says.
“Tony’s tradition.”

“Since Luc was in diapers.” Wes tips the go-cup at the water. “I came down with ’em a few years. Stood right here.” A long pause, the kind Jack has learned to leave alone. A towboat goes by upriver, all its lights on, and Wes watches it go.
“Don’t wait on nobody, podna,” he says. “I waited on God four years.”
He drinks from the go-cup and goes on looking at the water.

choices.key: At Spanish Plaza on Lundi Gras, Wes told you not to wait on anybody — he’d waited on God four years. You told him you’re done waiting.
response: Wes nods at the river. “Good.”

He finishes what’s in the cup and sets it on the rail, and then he and the Gentilly boys are moving off through the purple and gold toward Canal Street, and by the time the boat is in sight there is no bent brim anywhere on the plaza.

choices.key: At Spanish Plaza on Lundi Gras, Wes told you not to wait on anybody — he’d waited on God four years. You asked him if God ever came.
response: Wes looks down into the go-cup, at whatever’s left in it.

“Ask me in four more,” he says. He reaches over and lays his hand on the back of Jack’s neck, like steadying a kid brother at the top of a ladder, and takes it back, and goes off along the floodwall with his friends, and the crowd closes behind his hat while the boat is still too far off to see.

choices.text: “Is that a yes where you’re from?”
choices.key: At Spanish Plaza on Lundi Gras, Wes told you not to wait on anybody — he’d waited on God four years. You asked him if that was a yes where he’s from.
response: Wes laughs the old laugh, chipped tooth and all. “Where I’m from that’s a *sermon*, podna.”

He takes the back of Jack’s neck in one hand and gives it a shake and lets go, and then he’s off up the plaza toward Poydras with the Gentilly boys, and gone into the crowd while the boat is still a light down the river.

choices.key: At Spanish Plaza on Lundi Gras, Wes told you not to wait on anybody — he’d waited on God four years. You told him that’s a sermon where you’re from.
response: Wes turns the go-cup on the rail. “Where I’m from it’s a confession, podna.”

His hand comes down on the back of Jack’s neck, rests there a moment, and lifts, and he goes off with his two friends along the floodwall toward the Riverwalk, and is gone before the boat comes round the bend.

choices.key: At Spanish Plaza on Lundi Gras, Wes told you not to wait on anybody — he’d waited on God four years. You said nothing, and stood at the rail with him.
response: They watch the towboat. Wes taps the rail twice with the bottom of the go-cup.

When the barges are past he puts a hand on the back of Jack’s neck, for about as long as a nod takes, and pushes off the rail, and his friends fall in beside him, and the three of them go off along the floodwall into the purple and gold, well before the boat ties up.

s04a.slug: MONDAY · 5:50 PM · SPANISH PLAZA — A KING BY RIVER
body: The boat comes in as the light goes. It comes up out of the gray down the river all white, strung with flags from bow to stern and a crowd at its rail in purple and gold, and the roar starts on the plaza while it’s still too far off for faces, and comes back off the water doubled. Behind it the river has gone from brown to black without anyone seeing it happen, and the big bridge upriver is lit end to end.
Lena comes back up from the front rail with the twins. Josie takes one look at the crowd in front of her and one look up at Jack.
“You’re the tallest,” she says. “It’s not personal.”
He crouches, and she climbs on, coat and all, and he stands up with her knees under his ears and both her fists in his hair. Remy takes Jude. Lena stays at Jack’s side.
“He’s *old*,” Josie reports from up there, as the boat comes broadside.
“He’s always old,” says Remy.

On the deck, at the front, the King of Carnival stands in his crown with one hand up, waving, gold all down him, turning to wave to one side of the river and then the other, and on the landing the mayor waits in a dark coat with the people who wait with mayors. The band at the landing starts something slow and old that every Broussard on the plaza knows. Tony is humming it, flat. Remy is humming it, sharp. On Jack’s shoulders Josie is singing it, and Lena says, “That’s Rex’s song,” like that answers every question there is.

body.text: “He waved at me when I was nine,” she says, watching him wave.
body.else: “Rex waved at me from that boat when I was nine,” she says, watching him wave. “Right at me. I decided I was going to marry him.” The king turns to the other side of the river. “He was sixty-two. I’d have made it work.”

body.text: From Remy’s shoulders, Jude says, “We *know*.”

body: Men on the landing catch the boat’s lines. The king comes down onto the dock with his scepter up, into the crowd of dark coats waiting for him, and the mayor takes his hand, and the roar goes up again off the water.
Jack doesn’t tell her what Wes said.

Afterward they walk back up Poydras to the truck in the early dark, the family strung out along the sidewalk under the streetlights: Tony out in front with Josie by the hand, Remy herding Jude, Clovis jingling his keys, Theo and Margot arguing about Herzog, Laney with her arm through Kevin’s. Lena walks beside Jack. Her shoulder is against his arm the whole way.

s05.slug: MONDAY · 7:15 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — RED BEANS
body: Supper is red beans, because it’s Monday, and because it’s Monday it is also everybody. The leaf is in the table and the piano bench is pulled up along the wall side of it, and the windows over the sink have gone blind with steam off the pot, on since six this morning and watched every minute of the day by Mémère, who has earned the head of the table and the first bowl. Tony’s transistor stands on the sill under Julian’s roses in Grandmère’s cut-glass vase, tuned to WWOZ, and WWOZ is playing Lee Dorsey, and Tony keeps time on the oilcloth with the back of his spoon.

Tess is here with Beau and the baby. Lucille, two months old, sleeps against her mother in a knitted crawfish hat with the claws hanging down over her ears like a spaniel’s. Clovis has the far corner with his elbows out, and under the table Aints III goes from knee to knee taking up a collection. Luc’s chair is empty — Luc is on nights, downtown, working Orpheus — and Celeste has set his place anyway, the bowl turned upside down on its saucer to keep. On the counter, still in its bakery box, is the king cake: Jack’s debt, paid. Remy has asked about it twice.

Celeste has put Jack on the piano bench between Josie and Lena again, without a word to anybody. Mémère’s cornbread comes round in the black skillet, cut in wedges, and after it a jar of cane syrup that Tony pours over his own and no one else is permitted to touch.

body.text: On the counter by the stove, next to the bakery box, something sits under a clean dish towel, and the towel has been arranged. Kevin’s eyes keep going to it. Twice he opens his mouth; the second time it comes out. “Mrs. Broussard. It’s a Monday.”
Celeste doesn’t turn round from the stove. “Don’t you tell me what I can’t do on a Monday,” she whispers, and Kevin shuts his mouth and eats his beans.

Laney has run the house all afternoon, and is running it now, from her chair, with her eyes. There is a Walgreens bag in the pantry behind the rice that the twins have been told, on pain of death, not to know about. Halfway through her bowl she leans down the table and gives out the parts in a whisper, pointing with her spoon: the twins and herself on top, Remy and Clovis in the middle — “Side yard, eight forty-five, everybody but him” — and then the spoon comes round to the head of the table. “Altos,” Laney says. “That means *you*, Mr. Broussard.”
Tony looks at Celeste. Celeste looks at her beans. Kevin eats with his head down; he knows what day it is. Laney hasn’t once looked at Jack.
Kevin eats two bowls of red beans, asks for the Crystal, and says nothing else all supper. Jack passes him the Crystal.

body: Theo puts down his spoon and touches his napkin to his mouth. “Mrs. Broussard, I have eaten in restaurants with three stars and a sommelier who wept, and I would like you to know that these beans —”
“Don’t praise the beans, Theo,” Lena says. “In this house you eat them. You praise them, Mémère thinks you’re stalling.”
From the head of the table, on cue, Mémère looks at Theo’s bowl. “*Mange.*”
Theo eats.
Lena, without looking, spears the best piece of pickled pork out of Jack’s bowl with her fork, and eats it, and goes on listening to Tony.
“King came in on time,” Tony tells the table, of Spanish Plaza, as if he had piloted the boat.
“He came in eleven minutes late, Daddy. I timed it on Remy’s phone.”
“On time for a king.”
“Then he’s on Broussard time,” Lena says, “and we ought to put him on the payroll.”

Lena reaches over and breaks the corner off Jack’s wedge of cornbread, the crusty corner, the one from the edge of the skillet, and eats it, still talking to Tess across the table about the crawfish hat. It is the second thing she has taken off his plate tonight. He moves the plate a little toward her side of the bench.
“That’s two,” Josie says, from his other side.
“Two what?”
“Just two.” She goes on eating.
Lena’s LG lies face-up on the oilcloth by the cornbread skillet, and halfway through her second bowl it lights, and the little outside screen says JULIAN in blue.
She looks at it a second, and puts her spoon across her bowl. “Excuse me, Mama,” she says, and takes it out the screen door onto the back porch, and pulls the door to behind her.

Through the screen Jack can hear the shape of her voice and nothing of the words: low and even, a question, a longer answer, a pause. He knows that voice from the other end of a phone. He had it most nights over Christmas. The clock over the Magic Chef goes round four minutes while he eats his beans, and on the sill the transistor goes from Lee Dorsey to a DJ reading out the Orpheus route.
The screen door. Lena comes back in and sits down on the bench beside him and picks up her spoon.
“*Le chanteur*,” says Mémère.
Lena breaks her cornbread in half and butters both halves to the edges.

Remy has his spoon in the air. He looks at Lena, and at Jack beside her on the bench, and at the screen door with the porch light still on behind it, and back, and his lips move. He is a good-hearted boy and he has been doing a bit all week, and Jack watches the bit run out of road.
“Okay, hold on,” Remy says. “Brother-in-l—”
He stops himself. He puts the spoon down.
“…Okay. I’m confused,” he says. “For real now. Is anybody else confused?”
Josie doesn’t look up from her cornbread. “Everybody.”
Jude nods. Tony looks into his beans. At the stove Celeste says “Remy” in a voice so quiet it stops the clock.
On the sill the transistor goes on to the next record, and Lena reaches across Jack for the cane syrup, and Tony lets her have it.

body.text: At nine Celeste takes the dish towel off. Under it, on Grandmère’s cake stand, is a lemon pound cake with the glaze gone hard and white over the top and cracked across like a pond in Mill Creek Park in February, and when Tony asks, for form’s sake, where the doberge is, she whispers, “A doberge is for Sundays,” and that is the end of the doberge.

It has nineteen candles in it. Sunday’s box had five left; Celeste found the other fourteen in the junk drawer, in three colors, and among them a wax 7 from Jude’s seventh birthday, and she has stood the 7 in the middle, where it leans. “That’s mine,” Jude says. “You were *seven*,” says Josie.

On her way past the bench with the matches Celeste bends to Jack’s ear. “Next time you tell me the night before, baby,” she whispers. “A lemon pound cake wants a day. That one had six hours and a prayer.” She straightens up. “Don’t tell him I said so.”

Lena gets up and kills the light, and Celeste lights them with the long fireplace matches, one flame after another coming up under her face, and the kitchen sings: Tony a word ahead of everybody and proud of it, the twins racing him, Mémère in French at the speed of a hymn, Margot correct. Laney, who has kept a cold front over her side of the table all day, gets swept out of it by the time they reach his name and comes out the far side louder than anybody, on her feet, as if there might be judges.

With the light off the table is gold from the chin up and dark below it. Beside Jack on the bench Lena sings with her elbow against his, and Lucille wakes in her crawfish hat and decides against crying, and down at the corner nineteen little flames stand up in front of Kevin’s face.

Tony stands with the Abita. “Second time this week,” he says. “It’s still the rule. If you sleep under this roof on your birthday —” He points the neck of the bottle down the oilcloth to the corner where Kevin sits. “— you’re ours.”
“*Bonne fête, le maigre*,” says Mémère.

Kevin sits at the corner where he can reach the milk with nineteen candles burning in front of him and his hands in his lap. “Respectfully —” he says, and stops, and doesn’t go on. Beside him Margot puts her hand on the back of his chair. Kevin looks at the candles until the first of them drips.

At ten to nine Laney finds Jack at the sink and jerks her head at the pantry, and he goes. In there, between the rice and the Walgreens bag, she hands him Grandmère’s cake stand with Celeste’s lemon pound cake on it — Laney’s commission, Celeste’s cake — and lights nineteen candles off a single match, fast, one after another, her face coming up gold over them. With the last one she says, low, to the candles: “You told me. Not anybody else. Me.”
She shakes the match out and takes the stand out of his hands, and by the time she’s through the pantry door her face is back to February.

The light goes off on her signal, and the house comes in behind her in three parts. The sopranos are Laney and the twins and, without being assigned, Lena. The middle is Remy and Clovis. The alto is Tony, who has been told, and who sings it a full octave down, glaring at the ceiling, word-perfect.

Kevin is already wearing the sash — BIRTHDAY BOY, silver on pink, from the Walgreens on Carrollton; Laney put it on him herself at a quarter to nine. As the cake comes down in front of him she takes the tiara out of her pageant bag and sets it on his head, a rhinestone thing with real weight to it, and Kevin sits up under it with great dignity and doesn’t touch it.

With the cake down, Laney stands at the corner of the table and conducts the rest of it with one finger, cutting the altos off early with a look that could strip paint, and Tony, cut off, sits there with his mouth open on a note he was enjoying.
In the dark Lena’s elbow is against Jack’s on the bench, and she takes the harmony up a third over Laney’s, and Laney, still conducting, allows it.
Tony stands anyway, with the Abita. “Second time this week,” he says. “It’s still the rule. If you sleep under this roof on your birthday —” The bottle comes round to Kevin. “— you’re ours.”
“*Bonne fête, le maigre*,” says Mémère.

“Respectfully —” Kevin says, under the tiara, and stops there. Margot puts her hand on the back of his chair. Kevin sits very straight under the rhinestones and looks at the candles, and doesn’t blow yet.

At twenty to ten Jack and Kevin are on the curb by the Odyssey, with the house dark behind them but for the kitchen, and the street doing what Mid-City does on a parade night when the parade is somewhere else: a radio, a dog, somebody’s party two streets over arriving and leaving on the wind. Supper was red beans. Inside, it is still only Monday.

On a paper towel on the curb are two slices of the king cake, and in Kevin’s, standing up crooked in the icing, is one candle out of Celeste’s box from last night, which Jack took off the top of the refrigerator on his way out and will answer for. He lights it with his lighter. It’s only a lighter tonight.
Kevin watches him put the lighter back in his pocket. “Clinically,” he says, “you didn’t want one.”
“No.”
“Interesting.” He doesn’t say what it’s interesting of. He looks at the two slices instead.
“You understand the rules,” Kevin says. “Whoever gets the baby buys the next one.”
“I know the rules. I’m the one who paid.”
“I know the rules. Tony’s holding the paper on it.”
“I’m only saying. As a matter of public health. The debt transfers.”
Kevin watches the flame. “Bà Nội says I came on the first morning of the Goat,” he says. “My mother says I came at four in the morning and ruined her New Year.”
A siren goes, a long way off toward downtown. Kevin eats a corner of his slice with the candle still burning in the rest of it. “Celeste’s going to know about the candle.”
“Celeste knows everything.”
“Then she knows it’s my birthday.”
“She doesn’t know it’s your birthday.”
Kevin thinks about that. “Good,” he says. “Ours.” The flame stands up straight. There’s no wind on Dupre Street to speak of.
“And I’m adding interest,” Kevin says. “It’s my birthday.”

response.text: “Happy birthday, Kevin,” Jack says, down the table, through the nineteen little flames. Kevin blows them out all at once, and in the smoke, before anybody gets the light, he says, “Thank you, Jack.” His name, not Costigan.
response.else: “Happy birthday, Kevin,” Jack says. Kevin looks at him over the candle. “Thank you, Jack,” he says, and blows it out, and the wick smokes up past the Odyssey’s side mirror into the dark.

response: “Make a wish,” Jack says. “Not out loud.”

response.text: “I know how it works,” Kevin says. He closes his eyes anyway. When he opens them he blows out all nineteen, the wax 7 last, and the kitchen applauds him in the dark like a free throw at the buzzer.
response.else: “I know how it works,” Kevin says. He closes his eyes anyway. When he opens them he blows out all nineteen in one breath, the tiara tipping over one eye, and the kitchen applauds him in the dark like a free throw at the buzzer.

response: He has: it’s in his slice, a pink plastic heel sticking out of the cake beside the candle.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “I’m not buying the next one.” He blows the candle out and eats around the baby with care.

choices.text: *Cut the cake. Thin, the way Celeste showed you.*
response: Kevin blows them out. When the light comes back on Celeste has put the cake knife in Jack’s hand without a word, and he cuts the pound cake the way she showed him on Sunday, thin, wiping the knife between slices, and passes the first one down to the corner.
Celeste watches every slice go down the table and takes the heel of the pound cake for herself.
Jack doesn’t say anything. Kevin watches the flame lean and straighten, and Jack lets him; then it’s out, and the smoke goes up past the streetlight, and it’s Monday again on Dupre Street.

s06.slug: MONDAY · 11:30 PM · THE ATTIC — THE TIN
body: The box fan stands dead in the gable with the streetlight coming through its blades, and the light comes on through the vent and lays its orange grille across the rafters and over the roofing nails coming through the deck. Theo is asleep on the air mattress with his back to the room. By the hatch Kevin is asleep too, on his back, with his mouth a little open.

body.text: On the floorboards by his sleeping bag lies the wax 7. Somebody saved it off the cake stand for him.
The tiara is on his chest, rising and falling with him, catching the orange light in its rhinestones.
The plastic baby from the king cake lies on the top of his sleeping bag, face-down, where it fell out of his hand.

body: Jack sits up under Remy’s Tiger poster with the Carhartt across his knees and takes the tin out of the breast pocket.

It’s an Altoids tin from Pea Soup Andersen’s in Buellton, gone soft at the corners, with RELIQUARY on the lid in her hand. His thumb has worn the first R down to bare tin from riding on it in his pocket, through Christmas and Ohio and all of January, without his ever once deciding to. He has carried it to Ohio and back and across Texas, and he hasn’t opened it since Christmas. He opens it now, on his knee.

Eleven, packed tight, each Marlboro on its own slip in her lettering, and on top, on the curl of Andersen’s receipt paper, *No. 1 · 8/29/09 · the Lighthouse*. He doesn’t read the rest. He knows what they are. The smell comes up out of the tin with the lid, two months shut, and under it something he could swear is the inside of her coat pocket, and probably isn’t.
*If there’s one missing in January, I’ll know. If there’s one more, I’ll know that too.* She said it across a table at the coffee cart, the last morning before break, with one finger on the lid.

body.text: The pack is in the side pocket of his duffel, the one he opened on the front steps of St. Brendan’s in January. He shakes six Reds out of it into his palm and lays them in a row on the sleeping bag.

Hale’s legal pad is on the floor by the duffel, yellow, with THE SECOND LINE across the top and under it the one sentence he has. He tears six strips off the bottom of the pad along the blue lines, slowly, so the noise doesn’t wake anybody, so the sentence stays. For a pencil there’s a stub with BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD stamped down its side in gold, that came home in his coat from Banks Street on Thursday and never went back.

He writes in his own hand, small and slanting, the hand his fourth-grade teacher gave up on, not hers. He writes them in order, one strip after the next, without lifting his head. The pencil goes from the number to the date to the place to what it came after and on to the next strip, and the only sound in the attic is the lead on the paper and the house ticking under them. At the fourth strip the point snaps. He sharpens it with the little blade on his keychain, the shavings going into his palm, and puts the point back down exactly where it stopped, in the middle of a word, and goes on.

body.title: The first of six strips off the bottom of a legal pad, in his hand
body.text: No. 12 · 1/16/10 · St. Brendan’s steps, 3:20 p.m. · after Sully’s
Then the next, and the next, down to the drive. He lays each Red on its own strip, like hers, and fits them in on top of her eleven: yellow paper over her receipt paper. It takes some doing. They go.
Seventeen. He presses the lid down with the heel of his hand, and it shuts.
He has nothing to put in with them. He looks at her eleven a while in the orange light, and then he presses the lid down with the heel of his hand, and it shuts.
*If there’s one more, I’ll know that too.* Now she will.

body: Downstairs the house has gone quiet a room at a time. Somewhere toward downtown Orpheus is still rolling; once, faint over the roofs, there’s a band, or the wind with a band in it. The RAZR lies shut on the sleeping bag by his knee. The tin is cold in his hand, and then it isn’t.

choices.text: *Say a Hail Mary over it, for nobody you’d name.*
response: He holds it shut on his knee with both hands and says it low, slowly, start to finish, *full of grace* to *the hour of our death*, and puts no name in the middle of it.
He lies down on his back under the nails with the tin in the Carhartt on the floor beside him, and the last of the red beans comes up the hatch, warm and low.

choices.text: *Write one more strip — not a cigarette — and keep it.*
response: He tears one more strip off the bottom of the pad. With Tony’s pencil, in the same small hand, he writes *Wed 2/17 · Lent*, and nothing else, and folds it once and puts it in his wallet behind Frank’s folded note, where he’ll see it every time he pays for anything.
He lies back. The RAZR is a dark weight on his chest, the coat is on the floor beside him with the tin in it, and somewhere under all of them Mardi Gras is six hours off.

choices.text: *Put it back in the Carhartt and lie down.*
response: He puts it back in the breast pocket where it lives, and lays the coat on the floor beside the sleeping bag and lies down.

Under the nails, with the RAZR on his chest and the small hard shape of the tin in the coat at his side, he listens to the house settle under them, a pipe, a board, Mémère’s cough through two floors, until it’s tomorrow, and tomorrow is Mardi Gras.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 5:20 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — EYEHOLES
body: The twelfth morning, he says it at the gable window before anybody else is up, kneeling on Remy’s old comforter with the street still black below and the dead fan in front of his face: *He summoned the Twelve*, and on from there to the end, from memory.

Below him Dupre Street is already waking in the dark. Porch lights come on up and down the block, one and then three and then all of them, and a man two houses down comes out his front door dressed as a crawfish, or as a lobster, it’s hard to say in that light, and stands on his steps lighting a cigarette with his claws held up out of the way, and looks at the sky, and goes back in for an umbrella.

Downstairs every light in the house is on. Celeste, who hasn’t worked a Mardi Gras in twelve years and gets up at four for it anyway, is already dressed, with her gold bag folded flat on top of her head like a nurse’s cap, and there are grillades going in the black skillet and grits in the big pot and a row of thermoses on the counter with their lids off, waiting. Tony’s transistor on the sill has WWOZ, and WWOZ has the Wild Magnolias, and the drums and tambourines and the voices coming in under the chief’s fill the kitchen to the ceiling. Remy stands in the hall door in a union suit asking the house who has his other sock. Tony has thermals on under his Saints jersey. Out the back door the yard is fog to the shed.
“Long underwear,” Celeste whispers at each person who comes through the kitchen door, and she runs a finger inside Theo’s collar to check, and sends him back up to the attic for the rest of it.
The bags come in off the clothesline stiff as cardboard with the cold, and Celeste deals them out by the size in marker on the bottom of each, like report cards.

body.text: LARGE is his.
body.else: The one that’s left is LARGE, and it’s his.

body: Theo holds his at arm’s length. “I’m a paper bag,” he says. “I’ve turned down better parts. No.” Four minutes later he is wearing it and posing by the refrigerator with one hand inside his coat like Napoleon. Margot cuts her own eyeholes with a paring knife, precisely, measuring off her face with her thumb, and then sits down on the piano bench and reads Durkheim through them. “Margot Lindqvist,” Laney says, “are you *reading* in that?” — “He wrote it for exactly this,” Margot says, turning a page. “He just didn’t know about the bag.” Laney has commandeered the oilcloth and a tube of glitter glue and is doing hers in fleurs-de-lis, with her tongue in the corner of her mouth.

body.text: Kevin’s has a 19 on the back in Josie’s marker, a foot high.
Kevin’s has a 19 on the back in Laney’s glitter, still wet.
Kevin’s is plain. He wears it like everybody else’s.

body: Mémère wears no bag. Mémère sits in the kitchen chair at the head of the table in her Mardi Gras hat, purple velvet with a fleur-de-lis on the front in gold sequins, pinned at an angle she settled on under Truman.
Jack puts his on. The eyeholes Celeste cut look out, roughly, at the bridge of his nose and his left ear.

Lena has come down in her father’s flannel with her MEDIUM bag folded under her arm. “Those were cut for Luc,” she says, from behind him. “Luc’s eyes are closer together. Mama says it’s from squinting at Remy.” He hears the kitchen drawer, and then she is in front of him, two eyeholes’ worth of her, with Celeste’s kitchen scissors in her hand. “Hold still.”

He holds still. She puts her left hand flat on the side of his face through the paper to keep the bag from moving, and he feels her fingers on his cheekbone through it, every one of them, and the cold of the blades at the edge of the hole.
“Look at me,” she says.

He looks at her. There is one eye of her in each hole, close: a slice of Lena in the left hole and a slice of Lena in the right, her lower lip caught in her teeth, the crease the pillow left along her cheek, his black Bic still behind her ear from Thursday. The scissors go round the edge of the hole in small bites, close, careful, a sound like somebody shuffling a deck in the next room. She blows the paper crumbs off the rim, and he feels it on his eyelid.
He holds his breath through the whole of the left eye.
She moves to the right hole. Her knuckle turns his chin a little toward the light.
Across the kitchen Theo, in his own bag, has stopped posing.
From her chair Mémère watches all of it, with the sequins on her hat catching the overhead light, and then she says, to the kitchen at large, in French:

“*Elle lui coupe les yeux comme une femme coupe les cheveux à son mari. Et le chanteur au téléphone, et la Canadienne au téléphone, et ces deux-là dans le même sac. J’ai quatre-vingt-huit ans et j’y comprends rien.*”
Josie, from under her bag at the end of the oilcloth, translates. She does it line by line, clearly, as a public service.

“She says you cut his eyes like a wife cuts a husband’s hair. She says the singer’s on the phone, and the Canadian’s on the phone, and y’all are in the same bag. She says she’s eighty-eight and she doesn’t understand *anything*.”
The scissors stop.
“*JOSIE*,” says Lena.
“Grits,” whispers Celeste, and the plates start to go round, and that is all the answer anybody gets.
Lena finishes the right hole. “There,” she says. “Now you can see what you’re doing.” She takes her hand off his face and goes down the table to do Josie’s.
In the Carhartt’s breast pocket the RAZR buzzes against the tin. Ten to four in Burnaby, between setups.

s08.slug: TUESDAY · 7:40 AM · ST. CHARLES AVENUE AT JACKSON — ZULU
body: The fog has come up off the river in the night and lies in the live oaks along St. Charles at about the height of the second-floor galleries, so that the tops of the trees are gone and last week’s beads hang down out of nothing, purple and green and gold, dripping. Clovis’s truck has been backed up onto the neutral ground at Jackson from half past five with the tailgate down and the twins’ gold ladder chained to the hitch, and the Broussards stand around it in their gold bags with a little steam coming out of every pair of eyeholes.

Up and down the neutral ground the ladders stand in a line in the fog like umpires’ chairs, with families round them who were out before it was light — folding chairs, coolers, a man in a Saints parka stirring something in a pot the size of a washtub over a propane ring.

Celeste has hung the thermoses off the side rail of the ladder by their straps, in a row, like lanterns, and goes down the line with a sleeve of Styrofoam cups doing coffee rounds. Mémère has stayed home by the heater in her hat; Clovis will go back for her for Rex. Remy is asleep in the cab of the truck under the Saints blanket meant for Mémère’s knees, with his bag on.

On the tailgate of a Silverado three trucks down, a boombox is playing the Dixie Cups, and as far as Jack can tell it has played nothing else all morning, and the neutral ground wouldn’t have it any other way.
“You,” Tony says to him, and points at the ladder. “Ladder.”

So Jack holds the ladder. Jude and Josie are up in the gold box at the top of it with their bags on, swinging their sneakers over the rail, and the rig moves when they do. Lena is on the curb with Laney and Margot and Kevin; Theo is out at the edge of the street with both arms up, already complaining about the peripheral vision in a paper bag.

Lena comes over from the curb with a Styrofoam cup off Celeste’s line. Both his hands are on the ladder and Tony is watching the ladder, so she rolls the bottom of his bag up over his mouth with one hand and holds the cup for him with the other, and blows across the top of it before she tips it, and he drinks Celeste’s chicory out of her hand on the neutral ground with his bag rolled to the nose. When he’s done she rolls the bag back down and smooths it flat over his mouth with the back of her hand.
“I’m *right here*,” Josie says, from the top of the ladder.
Lena takes the empty cup back to the curb.

Zulu comes a little after eight. First the motorcycles, then a roar coming up the avenue ahead of everything else, and then the floats come up out of the fog one at a time, the fog making them as it goes: green and gold and black, palms and coconuts painted down their sides and a great papier-mâché head on the lead float, and the crowd going up on its toes. The riders, in the krewe’s blackface and grass skirts, lean down off the floats into the fog with their hands full. Out ahead of them walk figures in costumes Jack has no names for, waving at the curb like they know everybody on it, and some of them must.

A marching band goes by between floats, a high school from out in the East in purple and gold, the tubas steaming at the bells and the drum line so loud Jack feels it in the ladder under his hands. The noise is enormous. Beads come down out of the fog like weather. Josie catches a strand and Jude catches a stuffed something and Tony catches nothing and shouts at the riders by name, or by what he has decided their names are.

Theo takes a spear across the front of his bag and sits down hard in the grass. “A man in a paper bag,” he says, from the ground, to the fog, “felled on Mardi Gras morning by a spear. Sundance. Small release.” Kevin hauls him up by the back of the coat without a word, one-handed.
Then a rider on the third float leans down, a long way, one hand on the rail, and he doesn’t throw anything. He puts it into Laney’s hands.
It’s a coconut, painted gold, glittered, with a fleur-de-lis in purple on the side of it. Laney holds it in both hands against her chest and her mouth comes open in her bag.

She turns — to Jack, first, by reflex, holding it up for him to see, clean round on her heel — and halfway round she remembers, and her face shuts like a compact, and she finishes the turn the other way, to Lena.
“Lena. *Lena*.” She holds it up. “I have been *chosen*.” She puts it into Lena’s arms. “Hold this. With your *life*.” And she goes back to the edge of the street with her hands up for the next float.

On Lena, under the coconut, the Bacchus medallion is caught in its own beads.
Laney’s Bacchus medallion swings on her sweater as she goes, flashing in the gray.

Beside him in the box Josie spins round. “Tell her *WHAT*?”
