s08a.slug: TUESDAY · 10:40 AM · ST. CHARLES AVENUE — REX
body: By twenty to eleven Zulu is a noise somewhere downtown and a mess in the gutter. The neutral ground at Jackson is shin-deep in what it left behind: beads in the wet grass, a spear snapped in two, Styrofoam cups, the hairy brown halves of a coconut somebody dropped and somebody else stepped on. Last week’s strands hang in the oaks with this morning’s over them. Two ladders down, the man with the washtub and the propane ring has gone over to frying dough, and he sells it hot out of a paper sack for a dollar with the powdered sugar shaken in on top, and the sweet burnt smell of it drifts up the neutral ground through the fog, which is coming apart now, off the tops of the oaks first.

Laney sits on Clovis’s tailgate with her bag rolled up off her face to the forehead, as half the avenue is wearing them by now, and the coconut in her lap in both hands. “Her name,” she announces, “is Coco.”
“No,” says Theo.
“Coco *Chanel*. She has a last name, Theodore. She’s not a poodle.”

“You can’t name a coconut Coco. It’s beneath you. It’s beneath the *coconut*.” Theo’s bag is rolled up too, like a watch cap, gone soft at the fold. “I object on principle. It’s the first idea. You never shoot the first idea.”
“Kubrick shot the first idea.”
“Kubrick shot the first idea a hundred and twenty-seven times.”
Laney turns the coconut so the fleur-de-lis faces away from him. “Coco’s not taking notes from you.”

At ten Clovis unchained the ladder, left it with Tony, and went back up Jackson for Mémère, and she sits in the cab of the truck now in the passenger seat with the Saints blanket over her knees and the purple velvet hat on, its sequins catching what light there is, and the window down two inches, which is what she allows the weather and the parade both.

Rex comes a little before eleven, and the avenue knows him before it sees him: the block goes up on its toes from one end to the other. Masked riders first, on horseback, plumed, in satin, the horses stepping high and tossing their heads; then the floats, tall and old-fashioned, gold leaf over papier-mâché, swaying on their wheels; a great papier-mâché ox, white and enormous, riding by on its own float like the prize at a county fair; and then, high up on his float, the King of Carnival himself, the crown on, the scepter raised, turning to wave to one side of St. Charles and then the other. His riders throw doubloons that come down ringing on the asphalt, purple and green and gold aluminum with 2010 stamped on them, and Jude stamps on one with his sneaker to claim it, the way it’s done here, and Josie stamps on Jude’s.

When the king’s float comes level, Tony pulls his bag down over his face, puts his hand on his Saints jersey where his heart is, and bows to Rex from the waist on the neutral ground, a fifty-three-year-old fish man in a grocery bag, down as far as he goes. He comes up pink at the eyeholes. “The only king a Broussard ever bowed to,” he says.
In the cab of the truck Mémère lifts her handkerchief to the two inches of open window, and the king, who cannot possibly have seen it, lifts his scepter toward the truck.
“Every year,” Lena says at Jack’s shoulder. “Same bow. Same line. He told Father Hébert once it isn’t idolatry, because the king gives the city back on Wednesday.”

Between floats the cold comes back up out of the grass. It’s the wet in it; it won’t stay outside your clothes. Lena stands beside him in her jean jacket over her father’s flannel over long underwear, and somewhere between the ox and the king she starts to shake. Not a shiver. All of her, inside her own jacket, her hands up the opposite sleeves and her shoulders up round her ears and her teeth going, and she says nothing about it, because she has been to every Mardi Gras of her life and does not get cold at them.
The Carhartt hangs open on him.

response: He opens the coat.

He does it without a word, and without one she steps in, her back to him, into the warm he has been keeping, and he brings the sides round her as far as they’ll go and finds the zipper and starts it. It catches at her breastbone and goes no further. Her hands come up out of her sleeves and close over his on the pull, cold as the ladder, and stay.

The tin rides in the breast pocket over his heart. He feels her find it with her shoulder blade, a small shift against him. “You still carry that,” she says, to the parade. “Yes.” She settles back onto it.

choices.text: “It’s a large. Your mother said so.”
response: “It’s a large,” he says, holding the Carhartt open. “Your mother said so.”

Lena looks at the coat, and up at him. “Then it fits two,” she says, and steps in and turns her back to him, and he closes it round the pair of them. The zipper gets as far as her breastbone and quits. She puts her hands over his on the pull, both of them, and keeps them there, like it was hers to hold shut.

Through her jacket and his shirt the tin presses between his chest and her left shoulder blade. He feels her know it: she shifts off the corner, and then, deliberately, back onto it, and leans her weight there.
He takes the Carhartt off and puts it on her, over the jean jacket, and zips it to her chin.

She wears it for one float, a gold one with masked men throwing from the rail. Then she unzips it and takes it off and holds it open by the collar. “Arms.” He puts his arms in. She takes a fistful of the front of his shirt and pulls him to her, and turns round inside the coat with her back against him. “Don’t be a martyr,” she says. “It’s Mardi Gras.” She draws the zipper up herself, as far as it will go over two, which is her breastbone, and puts his hands on the pull, and hers over them.
The tin is in his breast pocket, and her shoulder blade finds it. She moves off the corner, and a float later moves back onto it, and stays.

s08b.slug: TUESDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. CHARLES AVENUE — THE TRUCKS
body: Theo and Laney have become extremely interested in Rex’s floats. Theo is explaining gilding to her, float by float, with both hands, and Laney is asking follow-up questions, and they have not looked toward the ladder since the ox.

Tess is three yards off at the curb with Lucille on her hip in the crocheted crawfish hat, antennae and all, and Beau behind her with the diaper bag. Between floats she turns round, and sees her little sister inside a boy’s coat on St. Charles Avenue with her hands over his on the zipper, and looks at her, and shifts Lucille to her other hip, and keeps looking.

body.text: Lena meets it. Then she unzips the coat and steps out of it, and turns round and zips Jack back into his own coat, to the chin, briskly, as if she were returning it to him, and goes and stands by the ladder with her arms folded and her teeth going. Two floats later Tess turns back to the parade. Lena comes back, takes the zipper down to his breastbone, and steps in.
body.else: Lena meets it. Then she takes the zipper down and steps out of the coat into the cold, and stands beside him with her arms folded and her teeth going. Two floats later Tess turns back to the parade, and Lena steps back in, and finds his hands, and puts them back on the zipper.

body: Rex goes by and on downtown with its noise in front of it. Behind it come the trucks, flatbeds dressed as floats one after another, families riding on them and throwing whatever they brought, beads and cups and stuffed footballs and, from one, a package of hot dog buns, unopened, which Remy catches and is proud of. The Broussards stay for all of it: Clovis at his cooler, Mémère in the cab with her window, the twins in the gold box with their arms out, Tony shouting at the truck riders by name, real or otherwise.
Just before noon Celeste comes down the ladder line to the young ones with her hands in her coat pockets and gives them the whisper she gives orders in. “Back by half past five or don’t come back.”
“Or come back,” says Tony, from the truck, “but come back hungry.”

s09.slug: TUESDAY · 1:10 PM · THE MARIGNY — FRENCHMEN STREET
body: It takes them an hour and change on foot to get from the neutral ground at Jackson to Frenchmen Street — down the back of downtown with the trucks still going by a block over, across Canal in a crush of people in feathers, along the back edge of the Quarter on Burgundy — with Remy in front, because Remy knows the way. He narrates the houses as they pass: who lived there, who got shot there, who got married on that gallery and to whom. Most of it, Lena says, is invented. On Burgundy a man in a full gorilla suit is asleep upright in a lawn chair on his stoop with a go-cup still standing in his fist, and three little boys no older than the twins are practicing on his steps, badly and gloriously, on a sousaphone and two trumpets, for an audience of their grandmother in a folding chair. Remy is lost by Esplanade and won’t say so, and at the corner of Esplanade and Royal Lena takes the lead without a word and he follows her and calls it his idea.

Frenchmen is a few blocks of old cottages and bars painted the colors of hard candy, with balconies, and every balcony is full, and the street under them is full of people in costume walking the same way, toward the Quarter. A walking krewe out of the Bywater is coming through with a brass band in the middle of it in sequined jackets, and they don’t march so much as move, the whole slow body of them, umbrellas up and turning over the heads, handkerchiefs going. A man goes by dressed as the Superdome, a silver dome of a thing from his shoulders to his knees with a Lombardi Trophy for a hat. A woman goes by as a king cake, purple and green and gold from her neck to her shins, with a plastic baby the size of a two-year-old strapped to her back. A man in long johns and a tutu and a Saints helmet. Two grandmothers in matching tinfoil crowns, arm in arm. From a balcony a man with a beard, in a wedding dress, is blowing bubbles down over the krewe with a wand the size of a tennis racket, and they drift down through the gray and break on the umbrellas. The light is gray and flat over all of it, and the cold has let go a little since morning, though not much.

And then, above everybody’s heads, the Holy Family, on stilts. Joseph in brown with a carpenter’s square over his shoulder, and Mary in blue with a white veil, ten feet tall and walking slowly, carefully, hand in hand, and in the middle a boy of eight or nine on shorter stilts of his own, in white, holding his mother’s hand up there over the street and looking down at all of it with his mouth open. They’re a real family; the boy has his father’s ears. The krewe makes room for them without being asked. A woman dressed as a crawfish crosses herself as they go by, and so does Jack.
Jack stands at the curb with his hands in his coat.

body.text: The sentence comes back to him in his own handwriting, off Hale’s legal pad, the one she read at the kitchen table and told him to keep: the edge of every crowd in this city for six days, his hands in his coat, watching it walk away down the street behind a horn. Here is the edge of one. Here are the hands.

Lena comes back out of the street for him. She takes his hands out of his pockets, both of them, by the wrists first and then by the hands, and walks backward off the curb into the krewe, pulling, and the sentence comes untrue a step at a time as he goes after her.
body.else: Lena comes back out of the street for him. She takes his hands out of his pockets, both of them, by the wrists first and then by the hands, and walks backward off the curb into the krewe, pulling, and he goes.

body: “You can’t write about it from the sidewalk, Youngstown.”

He is bad at it. He is from Youngstown, where a man’s body has two settings, the rec-league box-out and the kneeler, and neither of them is this. A second line is a walk that remembers it’s a dance every other beat, the knees going, the shoulders, a hand up with a handkerchief in it, and every soul around him has known it since they could stand. He stomps. He shuffles. He looks for it with his feet and can’t find it.

Lena pulls a red bandana out of her back pocket and puts it in his hand. “Wave that. Your hands need a job or they go back in your pockets.” He waves it. It helps. He gets less bad. For half a block he is very nearly something.
“Smaller,” Lena says, walking backward in front of him with her own hands going. “You’re dancing like you’re trying to get somewhere. You’re not trying to get anywhere. You’re just going.”
“This is Purgatory.”
“Purgatory’s got a band, Youngstown. Ask anybody from here.”

The band stops dead in the middle of the street for no reason anyone explains, and the krewe stops with it and stands there breathing and grinning, and then the snare goes off like a dropped tray and everybody is moving again. A big man in a feathered hat takes Lena away from him for half a block, spinning her, and gives her back with a bow. A woman in a tutu and a Saints jersey dances with Jack for a chorus and tells him he’s doing great, a lie and a kindness, and dances off. Theo is dancing with somebody’s grandmother in a purple wig, gravely and well, and at the corner he dips her, and she smacks his chest with her fan for it, delighted. Laney is dancing with Kevin, and Kevin can dance — loose and easy and dead on the beat, his windbreaker open and Theo’s phone still zipped in the pocket — and none of them knew.

Once, down a side street, Jack sees a Mardi Gras Indian standing alone at the corner in a suit of feathers and beads, pale blue as a pilot flame, still as a church, and then the krewe carries him past the corner and it’s gone.

Margot walks along the edge of it with Coco held in both hands like a specimen jar, not dancing, watching a street full of strangers turn into one animal. “Collective effervescence,” she says as the krewe carries Jack past her. “I told you he wrote it for this.”

Lena comes back for his hands. The street is wide and the krewe is loose and nothing pushes them; she only comes back and takes them, both, and holds them, and walks backward in front of him so she can watch his feet and tell him what they’re doing wrong.

body.text: He has had her hand all week — in his coat pocket on Carrollton, over his on the zipper on St. Charles — but never like this, in the middle of a street in daylight, with nothing making her. Her fingers are cold, and then they aren’t. She keeps them.
body.else: He has had her hands over his on the zipper of his coat on St. Charles, but never like this, in the middle of a street in daylight, with nothing making her. Her fingers are cold, and then they aren’t. She keeps them.

body: Down toward the river the band slows into something mournful, a dirge, the trombones low and the bass drum walking, and the krewe slows with it and sways. Without thinking, Lena steps into him: his right hand to her shoulder blade, her left on his shoulder, his other hand taken up in hers and held out, a waltz-hold, from habit.

body.text: “That’s a waltz, Youngstown,” she says, and doesn’t step out of it. “This is a second line.”
body.else: Then she catches herself, and steps back out of it. “Wrong dance.”

body.text: “You started it.”
“I *always* start it.”

For the length of the dirge they sway in the middle of Frenchmen Street in the wrong dance, her cold ear just under his chin and the bandana still in his fist against her back, and for the length of it he doesn’t think about anything at all, which hasn’t happened to him in ten days.

body: The dirge ends. The snare goes off, and the trumpet climbs up out of the slow thing into something fast, and Lena still has his hands.

response: He dances like he means it: badly, all-out, the bandana going round over his head, knees and shoulders and all of Youngstown thrown at the beat. The trumpet player sees him, swings round, and points the bell straight at him and plays at him, a high hard run of it, for his benefit alone. Lena laughs — out loud, up over the horns — and doesn’t let go of him.

He doesn’t let go of her hands. Not for three blocks, not for another dirge, not when the band turns toward the Quarter and the start of something fast takes the krewe at a near run, and not when she tries him with a little tug, to see. She stops trying after that, and walks backward in front of him the rest of the way.

choices.text: “Write this down. I’m going to need a citation.”
response: “Write this down,” he tells her over the trombones. “I’m going to need a citation.”
“You’re the citation,” Lena says, and turns him under her arm, which he is too tall for, so that he comes out the far side bent double and laughing with the bandana over one eye.

He finds the step — it’s there once he quits hunting for it — and keeps it, and gives her back her hands, and watches her dance. She dances with her chin up and her elbows out, as if the street had said something she means to answer, all the way to the end of every phrase the horns give her, which is its own education.

s10.slug: TUESDAY · 4:05 PM · ROYAL STREET, A STOOP — BEFORE CALL TIME
body: Where Frenchmen gives out at Esplanade and the krewe goes on into the Quarter without them, Lena stops, out of breath, with the bandana back in her fist. “Now you can write it,” she says, with her eyes on the next corner, and walks on. Remy peels off there for a cousin’s balcony on Esplanade, swearing on his mother he’ll be home by five.

The lower end of Royal Street at four o’clock is the quietest place they’ve been all day: Creole cottages shoulder to shoulder at the edge of the sidewalk with their shutters shut and their stoops two steps high, a gallery here and there hung with purple bunting gone dark in the damp. The Quarter is a roar with horns in it, a few blocks off and all around them; here it’s two dogs talking over a fence and a man hosing beer off his steps. Laney has bought Hubig’s pies at a corner store, one each, and the others are eating them out of the wax paper on the next stoop down, Theo and Margot and Kevin crowded together on the steps and Laney and Lena at the end with the coconut. Jack has the stoop above to himself, because that’s how the steps came out.
The RAZR goes off in his breast pocket. SKYE (MISFIT).
“Hey,” he says. “I’m on a stoop.”

“Don’t talk,” Skye says. “I have eleven minutes and a woman outside my trailer with a clipboard whose entire job is knocking. She’s very good. She’s a percussionist. I’m in a robe with sixty pins in my head. Tonight I get rained on by a truck for six hours. Glamour. Kyle’s left the Colts.”
“You told me Sunday.”

“Sunday he wore the shirt *under*. Today he walked in with the Saints on the *outside* and the horseshoe underneath, like a man who finally told his first family about the second one. Russ won’t look at him. They had to be separated at craft services.” A breath, for the timing. “And I showed the goose your picture.”
“What did the goose think.”

“The goose has views. The goose thinks you look like an expensive lunch.” And then she is the bag: a voice full of gravel and thirty years of Pall Malls, a Ralphs bag out of Studio City that has seen things. “Thirty years I carried that man’s groceries, sweetheart. Eggs. Coffee. The good bread. Not one thank-you. Now it’s Mardi Gras, now he wants to take me *dancing*, now I got *eyeholes* —” and the bag breaks down coughing, and Jack is laughing on the stoop with his head down between his knees.

“If you were here in it,” she says, and the bag is gone, and what’s left is low and close against the phone, “I’d take it off you myself. Slowly. Up over your head with both hands, so I could watch your face the second you could see me.” She gives him a moment with that. “That’s all you get on a workday.”
“You can’t say that to a man on a stoop.”
“I just did. Tell me about the parade. Not the floats. You.”

He tells her. The Superdome with the trophy on its head, the king cake with a baby the size of a toddler, the Holy Family ten feet up with the boy in the middle holding his mother’s hand over everybody, the band stopping dead in the street and everyone standing there breathing, the trumpet, the bandana. He tells her he was terrible and then less terrible. He tells her Lena walked him off the curb backward by both hands. She listens to all of it. Once, on her end, he hears the clipboard knock, and Skye says “Two minutes” away from the phone, and comes back to him and says, “Go on. The stilts.”

When he’s done she’s quiet a moment. “You know what you were, in the middle of that? Invisible,” she says. “A crowd that’s all facing the same way is the only place nobody can see you. I got out of a car at a premiere in Westwood once on the wrong side, the street side, and walked into the crowd instead of onto the carpet, and for about a minute I was just somebody’s elbow. Not one person knew. I think about that minute more than I think about the movie.”
He can see it: a girl in a dress somebody else picked out, ducking into a crowd like a kid going under a fence.
On the next stoop down Laney is saying something to Lena about the coconut, and Lena isn’t answering her.

“Okay. Tomorrow.” Paper rustles on Skye’s end, a printout. “I looked it up. Ash Wednesday, forty days, not counting Sundays, which is a loophole, and you know how I feel about loopholes. So tomorrow you give something up for forty days. What’s the theory? Is it training or is it penance? Because those are different *notes*, Jack, and I need to know how to play it.”
He turns the Hubig’s wax paper over in his fist.

“Both,” he says. “It’s forty because He went out in the desert for forty. So, training — the old word for what the monks did out there is an athlete’s word. You find out your body isn’t the one in charge. And penance, sure. You’ve done things. You want sorry to cost you something besides words. My nonna gives up coffee every Lent and is a holy terror till Easter, and she says she’s offering it up, and we all offer up Nonna.” He looks at the shut shutters across the street. “But if that’s all it is, it’s a diet with a rosary. You don’t give it up for you. You give it to Somebody. It’s a present. The going without is the wrapping paper.”

“A present,” Skye says. “That you wrap in going without.” She tries it again under her breath, the way she tries a line she means to keep. “That plays. What if you break it? Day nine, you cave. Is it over?”
“You start again the next morning. That’s most of it. Starting again the next morning.”
“That’s rehearsal.”
“That’s Catholicism.”
“I’ve never had a Lent,” she says. “I think I’d be good at it. I’m good at going without things.”
He has his elbows on his knees and the phone hard against his ear. On her end the knock comes again, two raps, the percussionist.

response: “Love you,” he says. “Go be brilliant.”
“Love you,” Skye says. “Bye, Bag.”

He shuts the phone. On the next stoop down Lena sits at the end with Laney’s coconut in her lap, looking up Royal Street at the balconies, at the gray over them. She doesn’t look at him. When he gets up, she gets up, and the six of them walk, and her hand goes up into one of the jean jacket’s useless chest pockets, two fingers deep, and stays there all the way to Esplanade.

choices.text: “You’d be good at it. You’d be good at anything you took seriously.”
choices.key: On Mardi Gras afternoon Skye called from her trailer to ask what Lent is for. You told her she’d be good at it — at anything she took seriously.
response: “You’d be good at it,” he says. “You’d be good at anything you took seriously.”
On her end there’s a silence that isn’t a bit, long enough that the clipboard knocks a third time. “Okay,” she says. “Bye, Bag.”
He folds the RAZR and holds it a while, and it stays warm in his hand.

choices.key: On Mardi Gras afternoon Skye called from her trailer to ask what Lent is for. You told her to give up the goose.
response: “Give up the goose,” he says.
“Never,” says Skye. “The goose is my *rock*.” The knock again; she covers the phone and says something to the door, laughing, and comes back. “Bye, Bag.”

He shuts the phone. At the end of the next stoop Lena isn’t laughing at anything; she’s watching a woman on a balcony across Royal Street take down a string of purple lights. On the stoop below, Theo and Kevin are fighting over the last bite of a pie, and Kevin wins it.

s11.slug: TUESDAY · 5:40 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — THE FAT IN FAT TUESDAY
body: The back door is propped open on a brick, and through it from the side yard comes the sound of the fat. Tony’s pork shoulder has been in the pit since five this morning, and every few seconds a drop of it lets go onto the coals with a hiss and a spit, steady as a clock in the next room. The transistor on the sill, for the first time all week, is off.

They are more than the table holds. Tony at the head with the carving fork; Celeste at his right, up more than she’s down; Mémère at the foot in the purple hat, which she has not taken off since five this morning and won’t till midnight; Tess and Beau with Lucille asleep in her car seat on the floor between their chairs; Clovis; Remy; the twins; Theo and Margot and Kevin in a row on the piano bench with their plates on their knees; Laney on the step stool; Lena; Jack. Luc eats standing at the counter in his NOPD blues, because he goes on at seven. The gold bags hang off the backs of the chairs by their rolled tops, LARGE on Jack’s, a row of them with their eyeholes on the floor. In the middle of the oilcloth, in a cereal bowl, sits Coco.

body.text: On the piano bench by Kevin’s plate is a saucer with the last of his birthday cake on it under a paper napkin, being saved, guarded.

body: Tony says grace standing, one hand on the back of his chair, in the voice he uses on the ice company: thanks for the pig, thanks for the rain holding off, thanks for the Saints, which he puts in every grace and will till they bury him; and for tomorrow, he says, give us the strength — and Celeste says Amen over the top of whatever was coming next.

He carries the shoulder in from the yard on a sheet pan with the smoke still coming off it and sets it down in front of himself like the Lombardi Trophy, and pulls it apart with two forks into long dark threads with the bark on them. “The fat,” he says, “in Fat Tuesday.” There’s rice, and a pot of greens, and two loaves of French bread torn rather than cut, and Abita for whoever is old enough to want one and a pitcher of Barq’s for the twins. Remy has set his hot dog buns on the oilcloth beside the bread, as a contribution, and nobody has touched them.
Mémère tastes the pork and says something in French, not to anybody. “She says it needed one more hour,” says Josie.
“It *had* one more hour,” says Tony.
Mémère says something else, at length.
“She says then it needed two.”
Tony keeps looking at the coconut. “In my day,” he says, “a Zulu coconut went on the mantel, and you didn’t name it.”
“Coco is not going on a *mantel*,” Laney says. “Coco is going to Dallas. Coco is going to have a life.”

At the counter Luc points his fork at Remy across the kitchen. “Bourbon at St. Ann. Stand there. They come down from Canal, and you get in front of a horse, I don’t know you.” He finishes standing, puts the plate in the sink, kisses his mother on the top of her head and his grandmother on the hand, and goes out the front with his cap under his arm.

Lena is next to Jack, because that’s where her chair has been all week. Her jean jacket hangs on the back of it under her bag. She eats with her left hand and keeps her right in her lap, and talks across him to Tess about Lucille’s hat, and Theo, at the end of the piano bench, is describing Rex’s ox to Margot as a piece of conceptual art, and Margot is letting him.

Celeste has not looked at Jack since they came in the back door at half past five, footsore, having walked it home up Esplanade. She has put a plate in front of him, and a napkin, and an Abita he didn’t ask for, and looked at the plate.
Jack’s RAZR lies face-up on the oilcloth by his plate. At eight minutes to six it buzzes against the table.

body.text: TELL TONY HAPPY FAT TUESDAY. MA SAYS DONT FORGET ASHES

body: Tony reads it over his shoulder, chewing. Then he lifts his Abita down the table at Jack, at the RAZR, at the whole state of Ohio. “Ohio,” says Tony, and drinks.
Celeste sits for the first time since grace. She takes the platter of rice from Remy and holds it, and looks across it at Lena, gently. “Baby. Is Julian coming for Easter?”
Lena has her fork halfway. “No, Mama.”
“Hm,” says Celeste. She passes the rice to Jack without looking at him.
Down the table Josie has watched all of this — the rice, her mother, her sister, Jack — with her chin on her fist. She puts the fist down.
“Are you going to marry Lena,” Josie says, “or the girl in Canada?”
The table stops. Remy’s fork stops. On the piano bench Theo stops chewing. Out in the yard a drop of fat lets go onto the coals, and every one of them hears it.
“*Josephine*,” says Tony.
“It’s a fair question,” says Jude.

At the foot of the table Mémère, who, Jack would bet, has understood every word, says nothing at all and reaches for the butter. Beside him Lena puts her fork down on her plate. She picks it up again.

response: “I’m in college,” Jack says.
“So no,” says Josie.

Tony laughs, once, and stops, as though somebody had kicked him under the table; somebody may have. Lena doesn’t laugh. She eats a forkful of rice, and another, and Celeste gets up for the hot sauce, which is already on the table.

choices.text: “That’s not mine to answer at your mother’s table, Josie.”
response: “That’s not mine to answer at your mother’s table, Josie,” he says.

Celeste looks at him. It is the first time she has looked at him all supper, and she does it with the rice spoon in her hand, the way she reads a pot for scorching. “Eat, baby,” she says — to Josie, or to him; nobody at the table is sure.
He looks at his plate: the pork, the rice, the pot liquor from the greens running into the rice.
From the foot of the table Mémère answers for him. “*Mange.*”
“She says eat,” says Josie, unasked, and he eats, and after a moment, beside him, so does Lena.

s11a.slug: TUESDAY · 8:40 PM · DUPRE STREET → ESPLANADE AVENUE
body: After the dishes the young ones go down for midnight, because that’s what Broussards do; Lena has gone every year since she was sixteen, and Luc went on at seven, in his blues, on the Bourbon detail. The twins are thirteen and not going, and take it as a crime. Josie argues the point at the foot of the stairs until Tony says her full name again, and Jude sits on the bottom step with his coat on anyway, in case.

Celeste holds the front door. She catches Lena by one sleeve going past, and Jack by the other, and gives them the whisper, both at once. “Midnight. And then home. It’s Lent at midnight whether you’re there or not.”

Remy drives her car with seven in it, which is against the law in two states, Lena up front with her hands in her jacket and the rest of them stacked in the back with Coco riding on Laney’s knees, and Theo asks Kevin for his phone and Kevin says “Midnight” before he has finished asking, and finds a place on Esplanade at the edge of the Marigny by a miracle he takes personally and talks about for two blocks. They walk in under the oaks behind him, the dark big trees and the beads in them, and down into the Quarter, into the noise coming up off it like heat off a stove; within ten minutes Remy has gone after a brass band toward Frenchmen and is lost to them, and nobody goes back for him.

s12.slug: TUESDAY · 9:20 PM · JACKSON SQUARE → THE MOONWALK
body: The cathedral is lit white from below, all three steeples, so bright against the low cloud that it looks cut out of paper and stood up in front of the dark. The lamps along the iron fence put a point of light on every spike. Inside the square the crowd has thinned to strays and costumes going home: a crawfish carrying his head under his arm, a carriage driver picking a strand of beads out of his mule’s harness, a girl in a tutu and a parka asleep on her boyfriend’s shoulder with a pound of beads rising and falling on her chest. Across Decatur the line at Café du Monde still runs out from under the green awning and down the block, and the wind off the river carries the powdered sugar across the street, and under the sugar the smell of the carriage mules, standing at the curb in a row with their heads down, done for the year.
Laney stops dead at the corner of the fence with the coconut under her arm like a football she would die before she fumbled.

“I need a Lucky Dog,” she announces, to all of them. “Right now. This minute. I have never needed anything so bad in my life.” She looks around the circle with real concern. “And so does everybody. Y’all are faint. I can see it on you.” She points up St. Ann with the coconut, where a Lucky Dog cart, a tin hot dog on bicycle wheels the size of a rowboat, sits steaming under a streetlamp.
She takes Theo by the sleeve of the good coat and Margot by the elbow.
“I have thought of nothing but a Lucky Dog since Sunday,” Theo says, going, already gone. “The chili. Specifically the onions on the chili. Specifically the raw ones.”
“I’m being abducted,” Margot observes, under tow, “by a woman with a coconut.”
Kevin plants his feet. His hands are in the pockets of his windbreaker. “Respectfully, I don’t want a Lucky Dog.”

“*Nobody* wants a Lucky Dog, Kevin.” Laney lets go of Margot long enough to hook him by the collar, and then she has all three, and they go up St. Ann into the crowd: the coconut riding high, Margot objecting in complete sentences, Kevin explaining to the general public that he isn’t hungry, Theo not looking back once.
Lena watches them go. “Subtle,” she says.
She doesn’t go after them. Neither does he.

It’s the first time in two days there’s been nobody else. The house on Dupre Street has more people in it than chairs, and somebody is always on the stairs, and all day there have been ladders and floats and bands and Broussards, and a paper bag over his head with eyeholes she cut. Now it’s the two of them on the flagstones in front of the cathedral with the crowd going by, and it goes unmentioned, and she turns toward the river and he goes with her.
They cross Decatur between a mule cart and a sawhorse barricade and go up the steps over the floodwall, and at the top there is the river.

He saw it yesterday from Spanish Plaza in the last of the light, brown and big and fast, and thought he knew what it was. At night it’s something else. It’s black, from here all the way across, and so wide that the few lamps of Algiers on the far bank look like a different town in a different year. And it’s moving. He can’t hear it — it doesn’t make a sound — but the light from the Moonwalk’s lamps lies out on the water in long shaking pieces and goes by, and goes by, level and fast and never stopping, like a belt in a mill left running all night. Upriver the bridge is strung in lights, and a freighter is coming down under it, lit at the stern like an apartment house with every window on. The Algiers ferry is halfway across, low and bright. The cold comes up off the water and finds every gap in his clothes.

Behind them the Quarter is roaring — all of it together, the crowd and a brass band somewhere down Decatur and a saxophone off by itself working through a song alone, a siren a long way off, a girl on Bourbon shrieking with joy at something — and they stand at the rail with their backs to all of it and look at the water.

body.text: “Christmas Eve,” Lena says, looking at the river. “You said you wished you were standing next to me.”
“You said come stand on one sometime.”
“You’re standing on one,” Lena says. And then: “Well.” She doesn’t finish it. The river takes the rest of it and goes on by.
“This is a levee, Youngstown,” Lena says, looking at the river. “You’ve never stood on one.”
“No.”
“Well,” she says, and looks at the water a while. “Now you have.”

body: She’s shaking. Her hands have been jammed in her own jacket pockets all evening, and her shoulders are up around her ears, and her teeth are going. He unzips the Carhartt and opens it.
She doesn’t wait to be asked this time. She steps in with her back to him, as she did at Rex in the daylight, facing the river, and he brings the coat around the front of her as far as it will go.
Then she turns around inside it.

It takes some doing. The coat is big but not that big, and she has to turn in place against him, one shoulder across his chest and then the other, her hair going under his chin, until she is facing him with the river at her back and the city roaring at his. It’s a small thing, a girl turning around in a coat. He knows while it’s happening that he’ll remember it longer than the parades.

His arms go around her inside the Carhartt. Hers go around him under it, her hands spread on his back through the flannel. The tin is in his breast pocket, and when she settles against him it presses into her at the collarbone, and he feels her find it again. She goes still. Her fingers come up and go over it through the canvas — the lid, the corner, the hinge — and go back where they were. She says nothing about it.

body.text: Her medal hangs on its mended chain where he fastened it, and he can feel the small oval of it through his shirt, over his heart.
body.else: Her medal is against his shirt, a small oval he can feel over his heart.

body: There’s no deciding. Later he’ll be sure of that. They’re standing at a rail inside one coat with their faces close because the coat is only so big, and she tips her head back to say something — about the freighter, he thinks; it’s coming on down the river behind her with all its windows lit — and doesn’t say it. And he looks down to hear it. It’s happening before either of them notices, and then they notice at the same time.

Her face is right there. Pink at the nose with the cold, a fleck of gold glitter off somebody’s costume caught at the end of one eyebrow, her lashes wet from the wind. Her breath is on his mouth, warm, with the chicory from supper in it. His hand has gone to the small of her back inside the coat and he never sent it. Her fingers have hold of his shirt. There is almost nothing left of the distance, and it’s getting smaller, and he isn’t doing it and she isn’t, and both of them are.
*Don’t wait on nobody, podna.* Wes’s voice, slow, the go-cup tipped at the water.

He wants her. He has wanted her on a porch and a pier and a stairwell at dawn, and he has never wanted her like this — with the river going by, and her mouth here, and nothing left in the way but him.
And he stops.

And in the same instant — not after, not because of him — he feels her stop. There’s no pulling back. There’s no moving at all. They’re held there, by each other, their foreheads nearly touching, close enough that he can feel the warmth come off her skin, and what’s left of the space stays exactly what it is, and neither of them lets go.

It doesn’t feel like anything he did. It feels given — put into his hands at the last possible second, from somewhere, entire — and under his palm at the small of her back she has gone still all the way through.

They stand like that. Her heart is going against him hard enough to feel through the flannel; his is no better. Down Decatur the band finds a song it likes and starts it over, louder. The freighter comes on down the black water with its windows lit, and the river carries it, and makes no sound.
After a long time, one of them is going to have to say something first.

choices.key: On the Moonwalk on Mardi Gras night you and Lena came within a breath of kissing, and both of you stopped at once, and neither of you let go. You said her name.
response: “Lena.”
Only that. Nothing on the end of it. He says it as he’d say it across a kitchen to see if she’s home.
She doesn’t answer it with a word. Her fingers close tighter in his shirt and take a fold of the flannel with them, and keep it.

choices.key: On the Moonwalk on Mardi Gras night you and Lena came within a breath of kissing, and both of you stopped at once, and neither of you let go. “Not like this,” you said, and she said it too.
response: “Not like this,” he says, into the little space that’s left.
“No,” she says. Her hands on his back don’t move. “Not like this.”
He feels her nod against him, small, her hair catching on his stubble, and nothing about the space that’s left changes.

choices.key: On the Moonwalk on Mardi Gras night you and Lena came within a breath of kissing, and both of you stopped at once, and neither of you let go. You gave her back her own word — “Well.” — and she laughed against you.
response: “…Well,” he says.
It gets her. She laughs into his collarbone, one short breath of it he can hear, and her hands, on his back, don’t let go of anything.
“That,” she says into his shirt, when she can, “was my word.”

choices.key: On the Moonwalk on Mardi Gras night you and Lena came within a breath of kissing, and both of you stopped at once, and neither of you let go. You said nothing, and held on.
response: He doesn’t say anything. He keeps his arms where they are, and his hand where it is, and lets the band on Decatur get through its song.
So she says it instead. “All right.” A little later, checking: “All right.”

s12a.slug: TUESDAY · 9:55 PM · THE MOONWALK — THE RING
body: She draws her head back far enough to see him. Up close, in the lamp, her eyes are wet, and he doesn’t think it’s the wind.
“Then talk to me,” she says. “All of it, Jack. From the start. From Becca. Don’t you dare skip anything, and don’t you dare let go.”
He doesn’t let go. He looks past her at the river a minute, working out where it starts. It doesn’t start with Becca.
“It starts before Becca,” he says. “It starts with Wes.”
“Wes.” She says it carefully, a step on the back stairs she knows is loose. Her hands tighten on his back.

“Columbus Day weekend, when he came out. Theo had a bottle of Jameson in the car, and Wes and I ended up on the ramp of the lifeguard tower at Campus Point at three in the morning, passing it back and forth. He told me about the attic. On Pauger Street. He told it like it had happened to somebody else and healed over.”
“It hadn’t,” Lena says.
“No.” He can see it still: the black water, Wes’s cap pushed back, his bare feet in the sand. “And then he took his phone out and turned it around and showed me a picture of a ring.”
She doesn’t move at all. Then: “Did you see it?”
“On a flip phone, at three in the morning. A little stone set up high. The band worn thin on one side.”
“That’s Mémère’s hand,” Lena says. “Sixty years of it. It’s back in her cedar chest.”

“Your mémère’s. Odile gave it to him at Easter, in her kitchen — put it in his hand and closed his hand up on it. *For when.* He was going to ask your daddy after you graduated. He said you had four years and a law school in you, and he could wait. He said, ‘I’m good at waiting.’ He said, ‘Don’t say nothing to her.’ And then he said, ‘Take care of her. She thinks she’s the one doing the carrying.’”
Lena’s face is turned into his shirt. “He said that?”
“He said that.”

body.text: “I didn’t answer him. I took the bottle out of his hand and drank. He said that’s a yes where he’s from.”
“I told him I would.”
“I told him you didn’t need taking care of. I told him you needed him to call at 8:04.”
“I nodded, and gave him back the bottle.”

body: He leaves out what Wes said yesterday at Spanish Plaza, with the go-cup tipped at the water. That one was said to him.

“And I believed him,” Jack says. “All of it. I thought it was forever, you and Wes. I thought someday I’d be standing in the back of Holy Rosary in a borrowed suit, watching. So when Becca asked me if the beach cleanup had been a date, I said yes.”
Lena is quiet. Up the river the freighter has cleared the bridge and is coming on.
“And then All Saints,” he says.
“Josie.”
“Josie’s texts. At the stove, with the soup going.” He can see it: her hand flat on the back of the phone on the counter. “She was so proud of herself for knowing first.”
“She still is,” Lena says.

body.text: “And the next night I sat on those stairs with you till the sun came up,” he says, “and I knew. I’d known for a month. Every time you said his name that month, I knew. You fell asleep on my shoulder sometime before it got light and I didn’t move for two hours — my arm went dead to the elbow — and the whole time I knew there was a ring, and I kept it.”
body.else: “You knew I’d known about the ring. I told you that much on the stairs,” he says. “What I never told you is why I stayed away after.”

body.text: “And at dawn I asked you what you were going to do,” she says. “And you said, ‘Whatever you need.’ And I said, ‘I know. You always do.’”
“And at dawn I asked you what you were going to do,” she says. “And you said, ‘I’m going to wait.’ And I said, ‘For what?’ And you said, ‘For you to be okay.’”
“And at dawn I asked you what you were going to do,” she says. “And you said, ‘Nothing. Not today.’”
“And at dawn I asked you what you were going to do,” she says. “And you said you’d get me a coffee.”

body: “I needed you to say anything else.” Her voice doesn’t rise; it builds, the way her arguments do, a sentence at a time toward the end of something. “*Stay.* *Go.* *I’ll be on the fourth floor.* *Call me.* Anything, Jack. Anything with you in it.”

He remembers the crease his collar left on her cheek, and the sun coming down the stairwell a step at a time, and how sure he was that he’d said the right thing. He meant *I’m waiting for you.* It has taken him three and a half months and a river to find out it didn’t sound like that.
“You know what I heard?” Lena says. “I heard a man who’d made up his mind. I heard you being good to me on your way out the door.”
And then, for a full minute, she is polite.

“Thank you for telling me,” she says. “I mean that. I appreciate your honesty, and I can only imagine what a difficult position it must have put you in. A man shows you a ring at three in the morning. What are you going to do.” Her hands are still on his back, but they’ve gone correct, a girl’s hands in a pew at somebody else’s funeral. “You knew there was a ring. And you let me find out from a thirteen-year-old.”
He opens his mouth.

“I’m not finished,” she says, pleasantly. “The next night you were official. I sat at Mrs. Vance’s table at the Harbor Inn with a linen napkin in my lap, and Becca put both her hands up over the bread basket — ‘He’s *mine*! Since the beach cleanup!’ — and Mrs. Vance turned that smile down the table and asked me whose I was. And I said, ‘Nobody’s, as of last night.’”

He remembers that table. The pianist going into the bridge and playing it through to nine people not saying anything. A sea lion under the window putting in a bar of its own. Lena down the table with her napkin in her lap, sitting very straight.
The courtesy doesn’t break. It runs out, the way a votive does, all at once at the bottom of the glass.
“And you sat there,” she says, “and let her say it.”
Her hands come round off his back and take hold of the Carhartt by both lapels.

response: “I didn’t trust myself single,” he says. “Your house had just come down, Lena, with a ring in it. If I’d been free that night I’d have kissed you on those stairs, and I wasn’t going to be the guy who came walking in over the boards with his hands out. So I didn’t get free.” He makes himself finish it. “Becca was a guardrail. Against me.”

choices.key: On the levee you told Lena about Wes’s ring, and that you’d wanted to be the one she came to after, not the one who was there when it fell.
response: Then the rest of it, because she said all of it. “I wanted to be the one you came to after. Not the one who happened to be on the stairs when it fell, so you couldn’t tell me from the banister. And I knew I couldn’t stop myself if I was free too. So I kept Becca.” He doesn’t look away for the next part. “She was a guardrail, Lena. Against me.”

response: He waits, with his arms around her. The band on Decatur goes into a chorus and comes back out of it. At last she asks it, into his collar. “Why didn’t you come?”

“Because you’d have said yes,” he says. “That night you’d have said yes to anybody who stayed on the stairs, and I wanted a yes from somebody who could say no. So I didn’t get free. Becca was a guardrail. Against me.”

s12b.slug: TUESDAY · 10:10 PM · THE MOONWALK, THE TOP STEP — THIRTEEN DAYS
body: Lena laughs. There’s no sound to it; he feels it go through her shoulders under his arms. “A guardrail. You used Becca Lindell as a *guardrail*.”
“I know.”
“She’s a lovely girl, Jack. She brought you *jam*.” Her hands stay on his lapels. When she goes on it’s lower. “…And I let you. I watched you do it and I let you.”
“And here’s the rest of that one,” Jack says. “The part I never said to anybody. I thought you knew.”
“Knew what?”

“How I felt about you. I thought it was obvious. I thought it was the most obvious thing about me — that you could see it from across a street, from the moon, from the back of a seminar room. I never said it because I didn’t think I had to.” He shakes his head over her hair. “That was the problem. The entire time. For both of us.”
She has gone very still against him.
“So when you said yes to Julian,” he says, “it felt like you saying no.”
She takes it in like a juror, without a face. When she speaks it’s the other half, and she says it herself. “And Becca felt like you choosing.”
“Yes.”
Behind them the cathedral stands lit white at the back of the square, and somewhere back in the Quarter a crowd is singing along with a band, badly, all of them at once and none of them together.

His knees have started to go, or the cold has got into them. Past the end of the rail a flight of wooden steps goes down toward the water, and below the steps there are rocks, and below the rocks the river. They get down onto the top step without letting go, and that takes some arranging: he sits, and she comes down between his knees inside the coat, turned sideways so her shoulder is against his chest and her face is tipped up under his chin, and he drags the Carhartt around her as far as it will go, which is not quite far enough, and puts his chin on her hair. It smells like Celeste’s kitchen, onions and coffee and the pork shoulder, and under that like the cold itself. The wood is wet. The cold comes straight up through his jeans. Close below them now the river slides by, black and quick.

“I ended it with Becca on the eighteenth,” he says. “A Wednesday. In Eli’s Ranger in the Portolá lot. She got there first. She said, ‘You were going to bring *her*.’ She’d seen it before I had. That night I told Father Osei I’d let her carry all of it so I’d never have to decide anything. Near enough the words.”

body.text: “And then you came into the lounge in your crawfish pajama pants with the Community Coffee mug and asked me if I was okay.”
“And you said, ‘Ask me again in a week.’” Her mouth goes crooked against his coat. “I never did.”
“And then you came into the lounge and asked me if I was okay. I said something. I don’t remember what. It wasn’t true.”

body: “A week,” he says. “That’s what I’ve been carrying around. That you were with somebody else inside a week. I yelled it at Laney in the laundry room in January, louder than I meant to. Theo said it back to me. ‘A week, Costigan.’”
“Thirteen days.”
She reads it back to him like a court reporter, every number in its place.

“Wes left me on All Souls. I said yes to Julian on the fifteenth. I told you myself.” She pulls back far enough to look up at him from inside the coat. “You want to know why Julian? Because he asked. Because I’d watched you choose — I *thought* I’d watched you choose — and not two weeks later a kind man stood in front of me and asked. He was kind, Jack. He stood up at Bastille in September and sang, before he even knew my name, and I walked out in the second chorus. And he asked me anyway. At Halloween I told you we were both waiting to be asked. So somebody asked.”
“And I wanted you to see it.” Lower. “That’s the ugly part. I wanted you to see me asked.”

Below them the freighter comes by. Up close it’s far bigger than it looked under the bridge — lit like a building lying down on the water, deck after deck of it, a man in a white hard hat smoking at the stern rail with the coal of it going bright and dim — and it slides past the foot of the steps, quiet, and goes on down toward the bend at Algiers Point.

“And three days after I told you,” Lena says, “you ended it with Becca.” Her hands have gone up her own sleeves, and she says it to the freighter’s wake. “Do you know what that *did* to me? I couldn’t tell if it was about me or if it wasn’t, and both of them were worse.”

“It was about you,” he says. “It was always about you. A girl from Idaho could see it on me from across the cab of her brother’s truck, and I ended it, and then I let the girl it was about spend three months not knowing that.”
Lena shuts her eyes.
All winter he has been sure she went first. From the sound of it she’s been just as sure, all winter, that he did.

choices.text: “I said ‘a week’ to Laney because ‘thirteen days’ sounded like I’d counted.”
response: “I said ‘a week’ to Laney,” he says, “because ‘thirteen days’ sounded like I’d counted.”
“You *had* counted.”
“I’d counted.”
One of her hands comes out of its sleeve and finds his under the coat, and holds on.

choices.text: “I was hurt you didn’t wait. I didn’t have any right to be.”
response: “I was hurt you didn’t wait,” he says. “I didn’t have any right to be.”
“No,” she says. “You didn’t.” Down the river the freighter’s stern light is getting small. “And you were.”
“Thirteen days,” he says. “You counted too.”
“I count everything, Jack. I’m a Broussard. We keep the book.”

s12c.slug: TUESDAY · 10:20 PM · THE MOONWALK — WHERE DO YOU GO
body: A long time after the ship is gone its wake finds them. The black water under the steps lifts and comes up the rocks white, and falls back, and comes up again, three times, four, reaching for the bottom step and not getting it; if it makes any noise, the city behind them drowns it out. Then the river is flat again and going by as if nothing had passed on it all night.

On the next bench a couple who have been arguing in whispers for twenty minutes get up and go, still at it, down the steps toward Decatur. “It was never your hat,” the woman says. “It was never your hat a *day* in its life.” The man says something about his cousin. In a minute they’re gone into the noise, and the Moonwalk is the lamp, and the benches, and the two of them on the top step.
“Two days after Becca,” Jack says, “Theo dragged me to a party in Montecito.”
Her cheek is against his shirt.

“He said it was to get me out of the room. It was because I was such an obvious mess about you that he couldn’t stand to look at me anymore. He lost me in about ten minutes. It was a house like a hotel. And there was a girl on a window seat in the corner, by herself, reading O’Connor for a part — ‘A Good Man Is Hard to Find.’ She had the grandmother down as a con.” He hears himself and tells the rest anyway. “I crossed the room to tell her she had it backwards. I’d never crossed a room for anybody in my life. We talked all night — O’Connor, the grandmother, whether a person can be good at the last second with a gun on her. She didn’t tell me who she was.”
“Of course he did,” Lena says. “Theo Vance’s idea of first aid is a house with a wine cellar.”

body.text: “‘Theo can’t be dragging you to Montecito every night,’” Lena says.
“He did it once.”
“Once was enough.”
“I knew about Montecito,” Lena says.
“I knew Theo took you somewhere,” Lena says.

“You asked me where I go,” he says. “At the Walgreens on Mission Street, at one-thirty-five in the morning, the night before St. Nicholas. You said, ‘Where do you go, Jack?’ And I said, ‘I’ll tell you sometime. Not yet.’”
She lifts her head off his chest. “It’s sometime, Jack.”
“You never told me where you went,” she says. She lifts her head off his chest.
“I’m telling you now.”

body: So he tells her. A house on Del Playa with the ocean under the back deck. Her car, an old Saab, parked at the turnout past the Marine Lab with the engine off and the windows going white. Most nights in December, till he went home for Christmas.

body.text: “The meteor shower,” he says. “You asked me, and I texted you *can’t, finals*.”
“To a meteor shower.”
“I wasn’t studying. I was with her.”

body: “And the night you texted me from the Brick,” he says. “‘Brick 8. Kevin’s asleep on his orgo. Practice? I’ll be Hale.’ And then, at twenty to two, ‘Never mind. Goodnight.’ I was in her car at the turnout. I read them both standing on the corner of Ocean Road at a quarter past two, and the eighth floor was lit from end to end, and I went home.”
She is very still against him.
“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I didn’t know what it was. That’s true. I’d sit in that car at the turnout and think, tell her Friday. And then Friday I’d see you on the fourth floor with your coffee and your margins and your highlighter in your teeth, and I’d think, tell her *what?* That I’ve been sitting in a car?” He shakes his head. “And because you were Julian’s, and it wasn’t any of your business, and I told myself that, too.” He looks out at the water, at the far bank, at Algiers with its handful of lights, and then back down at her, because the last part has to be said to her face. “And because I didn’t want you to know. That’s the true one. I didn’t want you to know.”
“Why?” she says. “Why didn’t you want me to know?”
“Because if you knew,” he says, “I’d find out whether you minded. And I was scared to death you wouldn’t.”
She looks up at him a while from inside his coat.
“I told you you were very hard to find that month,” she says. “I said, ‘You were very hard to find this month, Jack.’” She lays her cheek back down on his chest. “Del Playa.”
The cold is getting worse. She doesn’t move to get out of it, and he doesn’t move to let her.
“There were pictures,” she says.
He waits.
“I could stand the pictures.” She says it like a station of the cross she has been made to walk too many times. “Now there are the nights. All those nights in a car with the engine off.”
She stops there. Whatever she was going to ask next, it’s right there under his chin, and she hasn’t asked it.

choices.text: “Before you ask: more than there should have been. Never that.”
choices.key: On the levee you told Lena where you went all December, and the plain truth: more than there should have been, and never that.
response: “Before you ask,” he says. “More than there should have been. Never that.” And then, because she deserves the rest of the sentence, he starts on the rest of the sentence —

choices.text: “We never slept together. I kept that.”
choices.key: On the levee you told Lena where you went all December, and that you and Skye never slept together — that you kept that.
response: “We never slept together,” he says. “I kept that.”
She lifts her head. “And the rest?”
“More than there should have been,” he says. “A lot more than there should have been. And never that.” He starts to go on —

choices.key: On the levee you told Lena where you went all December, and told her to ask you anything. She asked, and you answered.
response: “Ask me anything,” he says. “I’ll answer it.”
She’s quiet so long he thinks she won’t. Then, without lifting her head: “Did you sleep with her?”
“No. Never.” He keeps his voice where it is. “There was more than there should have been. A lot more. Never that. If you want to know what —”

body: “Don’t,” she says, fast. “I don’t need it. I needed that, and I don’t need the rest.”

Her forehead goes down onto his collarbone. All the air goes out of her at once, the long way, and her weight comes onto him, and stays. He doesn’t say the rest. He keeps his arms where they are, and under his chin her hair is cold.

Upriver the bridge is strung in lights from bank to bank, and the wind has come around to blow straight down the water at them, and it finds every place where the coat gives out. She stays down against his collarbone. Somewhere on Decatur the band has gone into something slow, a trombone leaning on every note of it, and he doesn’t hurry her.
When she lifts her head it’s to look past his shoulder at the cathedral, three white steeples standing up out of the dark at the back of the square.
“Bastille,” she says.
“Bastille.”
He has never found words for it that he likes. So he starts with the name.

“The song was called ‘Magdalena,’” he says. “You know that part. You were there. Here’s the part you don’t know.” He feels her wait. “I’d been saying it. At your door, at the end of a night, when there wasn’t anything left to say and I didn’t want to go in yet. ‘Goodnight, Magdalena.’ And you let me. I thought it was mine. I thought it was the one piece of you I hadn’t got secondhand from somebody else.” The trombone holds a note too long and somebody down on Decatur boos it, fondly. “And then a man I liked stood up with a guitar, and it was his. He’d written it down. He’d put chords under it. It was on a set list.”

body.text: “You said it four times,” Lena says.

He looks down. Her hand has come up off his chest, and she is counting on it, one finger at a time, against the canvas of his coat. “The front steps of Delgado, two in the morning, in the fog. The Lagoon path, with the elevator doors coming shut — and I said, ‘That’s twice, Youngstown. I keep a tin for less.’ The library at dawn, with the bells going. And the front door at two twenty-five in the morning, under that little red light on the card reader.” Four fingers stand up under his chin. She doesn’t fold them down. “Lord have mercy.”

“You said it at my door,” Lena says. “In the fog, and under that red light on the card reader, and other places. I didn’t think you knew you were doing it, and I wasn’t about to tell you.” Her hand lies on his chest and doesn’t count anything. “Lord have mercy.”

body: “The first night,” she says, “on the rail. I told you who gets to call me that.”
“Your mother, the Holy Ghost, and Laney when she wants something.”
“And you’d known me about ten minutes, and you said it anyway, and I didn’t stop you. And then a man stood up in Bastille and sang it to a room. And I asked you to come.”

body.text: “At the Brick, at one in the morning. ‘Come tonight. And whatever you do, don’t leave in the second chorus.’ And you said —”
“‘I’ll stay to the end.’”
“And you stayed to the end. In the second chorus you found me across that room and you didn’t look anywhere else till he was done.”
“You came,” she says. “I asked, and you came, and you sat through every verse of it. What do you remember?” — “All of it.” — “So do I.”
“I thanked you for staying,” she says. “You never wrote back.”
“I thanked you for staying,” she says. “You wrote back *it was really good*, and I read it like a review.”
“I thanked you for staying,” she says. “You wrote back that Julian can sing and not to tell him you said so. I never did.”

“There wasn’t anything I could send.” He looks out at the bridge. “I walked home afterward with it going around in my head, and I couldn’t get it out, because it was good. That week I told my mother on the phone that a man wrote a song about a girl I know and it was good, and she said, ‘Which girl,’ and I asked her how the Browns looked.”
body.else: “It was all I could fit in a text.” He looks out at the bridge. “I walked home afterward with it going around in my head, and I couldn’t get it out, because it was good. That week I told my mother on the phone that a man wrote a song about a girl I know and it was good, and she said, ‘Which girl,’ and I asked her how the Browns looked.”

body: “Your mother,” Lena says, into his coat, “is a genius.”
She sits up inside the coat to see him. The cold gets in at her back, and she stays sat up in it. “I’m going to say this once and get it right,” she says, “so you hold still.”
He holds still.

“I asked you to come. I wanted you in that room. I told myself it was because you were my friend, and I wanted my friend to hear the best thing anybody ever made about me.” She stops, and starts again lower. “I’ve had two months to work out what I really wanted you there for, and I don’t like the answer. I wanted to watch your face while he sang it. I wanted to see what it would do. And I saw. And that’s when everything turned over, Jack. Not for him. For me. Watching you hear it.” Her eyes are wet and they stay on his. “I’m sorry. I am so sorry I asked you.”

body.text: “And then the Advent party,” she says, before he can find anything to say back. “Theo’s contraband mistletoe taped up on the kitchen doorframe, and Julian kissed my cheek under it, and you looked. Once. You had Father Osei’s dish towel over your shoulder and a wet cup in your hand, and you looked up from the cup, and I saw it go into you.” She stops on that. “That’s when I started deciding.”

body: “The night before the shuttle I knocked on your door with two coffees from the urn and an index card in my pocket. Every stop on it was somewhere I’d been with you.” Down Decatur the trombone gives up and a clarinet takes the song away from it. “That card was as honest as I knew how to be in December, and you never once asked me why.”
He saw the top line upside down in his doorway — *1. DELGADO — DOWNSTAIRS* — and put it out of his head, because not asking was easier than finding out. “I was scared of what you’d say,” he says.

body.text: “And the roof,” she says. “You said, ‘I’m in —’”
“And you said, ‘Jack.’”

“I said your name so you’d stop.” She says it straight up into his face. “Because if you’d finished it I’d have answered it. On a roof. With a van coming at a quarter to five and somebody else’s song still going in Oakland.”
He stood on that gravel with the rest of it in his mouth and let her stop him, and all winter he’s been sure she stopped him because the answer was no.

“And the roof,” she says. “You didn’t say anything up there. Whatever it was. If you had, I’d have answered it, and I don’t know what that would have done to either of us, with a van coming at a quarter to five.”
“What did you say at the airport?” he asks. “At the corner, where the hall turns. The PA ate it.”
“*Ero cras*, you idiot.” She says it into his shirt. “I *taught* it to you.”
He can see it on the glass of the Newman door, his own finger going up the column from the bottom, letter by letter. *Tomorrow I will be there.*
“What did you say at the airport?” he asks. “At the corner, where the hall turns. The PA ate it.”
“*Ero cras*.” She says it into his shirt. “It’s on Father Osei’s door at the end of Advent, upside down, if you read the antiphons from the bottom. *Tomorrow I will be there.*”
“I meant January,” Lena says. “I meant when you got back I’d be there.” She doesn’t lift her head. “And you got off a plane three weeks later and kissed somebody at a rope.”
There’s nothing that goes after that, and he doesn’t try to put anything there.

body: The cold has got worse. She sits back up and looks at him, and when she speaks it has the old courtroom snap in it, turned inside out.
“Magdalena is going to say something now,” she says, “and you’re going to let her finish it.”
“Okay.”
“At my grandmother’s tomb I told you who calls me that. Grandmère. Mémère, when I’m in trouble. Father Hébert, because he poured the water.”

body.text: “Professor Hale, once, and I fixed that.”

body: Her hand is up between them, counting, a finger for each of them against the canvas of his coat, and one finger is still folded down, waiting.
“— and —”
The clarinet on Decatur finishes. In the space it leaves there’s the hum of the lamp, and the city further off, and her.
“— and you.”

choices.text: *Say her name. The whole of it.*
choices.key: On the levee Lena told you she was sorry she asked you to come hear the song. You said her whole name, and she let it stand.
response: “Magdalena.”
Not *goodnight*. There’s no door behind her, and nobody going in. He says it because it’s hers and because she just gave it to him, and it goes out over the black water and doesn’t come back.
She lets it stand. The last finger stays up between them, and she doesn’t fold it down.

choices.text: “It was the worst night of my life, and I stayed, because you asked.”
choices.key: On the levee Lena told you she was sorry she asked you to come hear the song. You told her it was the worst night of your life, and you stayed because she asked.
response: “It was the worst night of my life,” he says. “And I stayed, because you asked.”
“I know,” she says. “I watched you do it. Every verse.” She folds the counting hand shut, finger by finger, around nothing.

choices.text: “It was a good song. That was the worst part.”
choices.key: On the levee Lena told you she was sorry she asked you to come hear the song. You told her it was a good song, and that was the worst part.
response: “It was a good song,” he says. “That was the worst part.”
“It was a *really* good song,” she says, miserable, with her eyes still wet, and puts her face back down against his collar.

s12e.slug: TUESDAY · 10:45 PM · THE MOONWALK — CALL ME AFTER
body: Lena stays down a while longer. When she moves, she turns. She comes around inside the coat on the step below him until she’s facing him between his knees, with the Carhartt held around her shoulders by his arms, and she puts both hands flat on his chest, side by side, over his heart. He has seen her put her hands on a seminar table like that, right before she takes the table apart.
“Christmas,” she says.
“I called you most nights.”

body.text: “Every night. I said it at Hale’s, in front of everybody.” And she says it again, word for word, only lower: “‘Every night, Jack. From your daddy’s garage. I sat out on my mama’s back steps in a coat in the dark so I wouldn’t wake the house, and you read me my own margins, and you told me about your brother and your grandmother and the snow, and I told you —’”
body.else: “Every night,” she says. “At Hale’s I said *every single day*. It was every night. From your daddy’s garage. I sat out on my mama’s back steps in a coat in the dark so I wouldn’t wake the house, and you read me my own margins, and you told me about your brother and your grandmother and the snow, and I told you —”

body.text: At Hale’s she stopped there, with the table watching. Here there’s only him.
body.else: She stops there, the way she would have stopped with a table watching. Here there’s only him.

body: “And I told you about Mémère’s hip, and the bonfires on the levee at Lutcher, and Daddy’s knee in the cold room, and what Father Hébert said about the Holy Innocents,” she says. “I told you every single thing but one. I was out on those steps every night deciding something, with you in my ear, and I never said what.”

“Three times I told you he was coming,” Lena says. “‘Julian lands the thirtieth. Mémère’s ironing a tablecloth.’ ‘Julian lands tomorrow at four.’ ‘The gumbo happened. Mémère ironed the tablecloth twice.’ And every time I stopped after, and waited. Three times I told you, and three times you let me hang there.”
“What was I supposed to say? *Don’t?*”
“Yes.”

He sat in a cold garage with the phone against his ear and heard her read him the weather in a town he’d never see, and it didn’t once cross his mind that she was standing at the end of every forecast waiting for him to say a word.

body.text: “New Year’s,” he says. “Your text came in the second my phone turned one. *Happy New Year, Jack. —L.* I typed back *1:00. not 1:01. i saw.* And I erased it.” He has never told anybody that. “I sat there and took it out.”
“I sent it at 12:59,” Lena says, “so it would land on your minute.”
“New Year’s,” he says. “I wrote you back.” — “*happy new year lena*,” she says. “No capitals. I read it forty times on the back steps and I couldn’t make it say one thing more than that.”
“New Year’s,” he says. “Your text came, and I didn’t answer it. I held the phone till two.” — “I know you didn’t answer it,” she says. “I was holding mine.”

body: For a little there’s only the cold.
“I’d decided,” she says. “Over Christmas. After the party — after your face under that doorframe — and because of those calls, every one of them. I’d decided to end it with Julian.”

body.text: Two pieces of a sentence he caught through a door in January — *she’d decided, Theo* — *over Christmas* — and carried around since in two halves, come together in his head and make one, and he hears it whole.

body: “Say it,” she says. “The call. Laney made me say it to her four times in the bathroom with the fan going so the hall couldn’t hear. I bet somebody made you.”
“Theo. While I was doing my tie.”
So they say it. She does her lines and he does his, on the top step of the Moonwalk with the Quarter roaring at his back, and they don’t have to stop and think for any of it.
“‘I’m going to see him Monday. Dinner, after Hale. Will you be around after? Monday night. Nine, ten.’”
“‘Probably not. I’ve got a thing.’”
“‘Okay. Then call me after. Eat something first.’” She doesn’t take her eyes off him for the next one. “‘I haven’t been fair to him, Jack. I’ve known it a while. I’m going to fix it.’”

body.text: “‘Okay.’”
“‘Lord, he speaks.’”
“‘He’s a good guy, Lena. He deserves that.’”
“‘He does.’”
“‘Why are you telling me?’”
“And I didn’t tell you why,” she says. “That’s on me.”
“‘Fix it how? Write him a song?’”
“‘That’s not funny.’”

body: “*Fix it*,” Lena says. “End it. *After* — after I’d ended it, Monday night, at that dinner. *Call me after.*” Her hands press once against his chest. “Be there after, Jack. That’s what I said. I asked a man to be up at ten o’clock on a Monday night waiting to hear how my dinner with another man went. Who asks that? Who asks that of a *friend*?”
“I heard *fix it*,” he says. “Make it right. With him. I heard *call me after* the way you’d say it to a cousin. I heard you shutting a door on me, real gentle, so it wouldn’t wake anybody.”
She opens her mouth to win it. She gets as far as the first word, and stops, and her eyes go off him to the river and come back.
“I said *fix it*,” she says. “I said *fix it*. Who says *fix it* about a breakup?” She shuts her eyes. “I sounded like Daddy talking about a carburetor.”
It gets out of him, one short laugh, up at the low cloud, and it gets out of her too, out loud, the first time tonight, with her eyes still shut, and her hands knock against his chest for it.
“Now you,” she says, opening them. “Tell me about your thing.”

“There wasn’t any thing.” It costs more than he thought, said up close. “I said it so I wouldn’t be sitting by a phone Monday night while you fixed it. And by Monday night —” He makes himself. “By Monday night my thing was Del Playa.”
Her hands stay where they are.

“The next day I got off a plane,” he says, “and there was a sign at the gate in eyeliner, and I kissed her under it, and a girl in the line filmed it. Sunday she set the status, and I said yes to it.”
“I landed Sunday at four,” Lena says. “By Sunday night I’d seen both.”

She looks at him, close, with her hands on him.
“I found out from a status,” she says, “after we talked every single day for weeks.”

“I couldn’t tell you,” he says, “without telling you what the calls had been. And I thought you’d told me, on that phone, that you were going back to him. I thought you’d told me nicely. There wasn’t anything I could say that you’d want to hear.”

“You could have tried me.” Her hands press harder. “You could have called me Saturday from the airport parking lot. You could have texted me from the plane. *I’m seeing somebody. I wanted you to hear it from me.* I’d have hated you for a week, Jack, and I’d have hated you to your face, on the phone, like a friend. You owed me that much before you owed the internet anything.”
There isn’t an argument against it, and he doesn’t make one. “I did,” he says. “I owed you that.”
“You did.” She keeps it a moment, won. Then, quieter: “And I’d have hung up on you.”
“I know.”

body.text: “And then Hale’s,” she says.

He gives her his own line back, the worst one, because it’s his to carry. “‘That right there. That’s what I meant in San Francisco. You as good as told me to do what I did. I didn’t realize I owed you proof of delivery.’”
“‘I said no such thing,’” Lena says. “And you called me a liar, and I called you one, at Hale’s table, with Hale at the head of it.”
“You called me a liar in front of Caleb Hargrove.”
“You called me one in front of Hale’s *dog*.”
“The dog took your side.”
“Berkeley’s *deaf*, Jack. Berkeley takes everybody’s side.”

It’s funny. For about as long as a breath it’s the funniest thing either of them has ever heard. And then it isn’t, because it was a real table with real people around it, and they said it to each other’s faces and both of them believed it.
“And all of January,” she says, “you walked around thinking I was a liar, and I walked around thinking you were one. On the curb I as good as said it to your face.”

“And I wasn’t. I said what I said.” Her hands haven’t left him, and her eyes are wet again, and her face could go either way, into a laugh or the other thing. “That’s the stupidest part.”

“Dido,” Lena says. “The eleventh.”

“I moved it out of the Fishbowl,” Lena says, “and you never asked me why, so here’s why. I wasn’t going to sit in my own booth and watch her in my bar.”

Me and him. I thought you were sitting up there on the fourth floor putting something in it a drop at a time, on purpose, so I’d have to watch it go.”
“If I’d come down that night,” Lena says, “I’d have told you to stop whatever you were doing. I thought you were taking it apart, me and him. A drop at a time. On purpose.”

She looks at him, and leaves it.
“The curb,” she says. “After the Walk.”
“‘How do you have the nerve to be mad at me? For any of this?’”

body: “And you said, ‘Thank you for coming, Jack,’ and left.”

“And I was right to leave,” she says. “You don’t get to be mad at me, Jack. Not then. You had a girl on your arm in every picture on the internet, and you stood on a curb in front of a van full of people and asked me where I got the *nerve*. I was the one who’d been left on a phone. You don’t get to be the one who’s hurt in front of a van.”

She’s right, and he knows the shape of it from the inside: he stood on that curb and made himself the wronged party because it was easier than being the one who went to Del Playa. “No,” he says. “I didn’t get to be.”
“You were mad at me for a gate and a status,” she says. “I was mad at you for a *thing*, and for three times on a phone.”

“You found the one thing,” he says. “On the first try.” And because it’s true, and she ought to have it: “I didn’t go up that Sunday. I knelt.”
Her hands stop on his chest. “I’m sorry,” she says. “That one I’m sorry for. That one was low, and I went looking for it.”
“‘You can’t forgive a *Facebook status*,’” he says. Equal time.
“And you found mine,” she says.
“We said things at that table I’d take back out of the transcript if I could,” she says. “Both of us.” — “Both of us.”
