“Hale stood up. I didn’t know the man could get up that fast.”
“And Monday, ‘The Dead,’” he says. “Hale throwing it straight at us like a pitching machine.”

“And six minutes behind his door,” she says, “and I came out and walked right by you.” She shakes her head. “He asked me if I was all right. Hale. In that voice. And I said, ‘Perfectly, thank you,’ and I could hear how I sounded, and so could he, and he let me go anyway. I was terrified of him for a week.”
“And Thursday we packed a van through Kevin and Laney.”
“And then the drive.”
She’s quiet. Her hands have gone still. “I went after her,” she says. “In the van. I called her a performer. I said it every way I knew how, and I know a lot of ways.”
“And I was as angry as I’ve ever been in my life.”

body.text: “And you said,” Lena says, and she has it by heart, every word: “‘Sorry, I forgot how private you and Julian are. When she stars in a movie called “Jack” I’ll make sure you come watch the whole thing next to me so we can see your face enjoying how authentic and humble everything is.’”
Hearing it in her mouth is worse than saying it was.
“That line about the movie was the meanest thing anybody’s ever said to me,” she says. “And it was fair.”
“It wasn’t fair.”
“It was fair enough to shut me up for the whole of West Texas.”
“And you shut your mouth on whatever you had,” she says, “and kept it shut for the whole of West Texas. I watched you hold it. Tell me what it was.” — “That you were jealous.” — “I was.”

body: He looks at it all laid out, January to the Texas line. Dido and Sarah Miles and Gretta Conroy at her window in the snow, a Facebook status, and a woman in Vancouver who was never what any of it was about. They fought about every bit of it.
“We had a war about *Dido*,” Lena says.
“Aeneas had a fleet.”
“He had a *choice*.”
“So did she.”

They look at each other. And it’s funny — it’s so stupid it’s funny, two people who talked every night for three weeks spending a month going at each other in front of their professor by way of a dead queen of Carthage — and he laughs, really laughs, out over the water, and she says, “Don’t you laugh at Dido,” with her eyes running and her mouth not minding her at all. And then it isn’t funny, because it was a month, and it was them. And then, because it was *Dido*, it is again.

response: “We had a war by proxy,” he says. “Aeneas lost.”
“Aeneas *won*, Jack.” She’s wiping her eyes with the heel of one hand and keeping the other on him. “That’s the whole problem with the poem.”
“Then I’m sorry about the movie line.”
“I’m sorry about *performing*.” She says it to his face, both words. “Now we’re even, and I hate it.”

response: “Every one of them was the phone call,” he says.
“Every one,” she says. “Even Dido.” She looks down at her own hands on his shirt as if they belonged to somebody who’d been in all those rooms. “I’m sorry about *performing*.”
“I’m sorry about the movie.”
“I’m sorry about the movie line.”
“Don’t be. I’m sorry about *performing*. She isn’t. She’s —”
And Lena stops herself there, with her mouth open on the rest of it, and shuts it, and shakes her head once at him: not yet.

s12g.slug: TUESDAY · 11:05 PM · THE MOONWALK, IN THE FOG — LUCKY DOGS
body: The fog comes off the river without any warning. Algiers is there across the water with its handful of lamps, and then it’s a smear, and then it’s gone, and the fog is coming up the rocks and over the lowest steps in a slow white roll, and the Moonwalk lamp has a ring around it. Behind them the cathedral goes soft at the edges. The cold turns wet and gets into the canvas.
“Theo,” Jack says.
“Laney,” Lena says, at the same time.
They look at each other in the fog.

“He made me say the call to him,” Jack says. “Then he asked me what the thing was, folding socks. He said ‘A week, Costigan’ back to me like a scouting report. He said, ‘Over Christmas. You called her every night.’ I said most nights. And then he stood in our room with the Saints schedule and said ‘once in a lifetime’ till I said yes to New Orleans to make him stop.”

“And Laney wrote mine down,” Lena says. “She had a legal pad. She’d come in at two in the morning and sit on the end of my bed in her retainer and say, ‘Tell me the phone call again, sugar,’ and I’d tell it, and she’d make a face like a judge at a pie contest. ‘He said he had a *thing*?’ Every time. Like it was new.”

“They had a whiteboard. I walked in on them in the lounge in January and it went over on its swivel so fast it squealed. There was a word on the back in pink. FACTS. Theo said they were planning Laney’s birthday.”
“Laney’s birthday was a doberge on Mama’s cake stand,” Lena says. “Nobody needed a whiteboard for that.”

body.text: “She told me what you said,” Lena says. “At the dryer. She came upstairs that night and told me. ‘She was really upset, Jack, and she didn’t have anyone.’ And you said, ‘Yeah, well. So was I.’”
“I did.”
“I didn’t believe her. Laney lies for sport. She said you said it at a *dryer*.” Lena’s hands go up, appealing to the fog. “Who says that at a dryer?”
“I did. I said it at a dryer.”
“Laney told me something you said, in January,” Lena says. “I didn’t believe her. Laney lies for sport.” — “Whatever it was,” he says, “I said it.”
“Theo knew how bad it was,” he says. “I told him.”

body: “Laney turned around this morning at Zulu with that coconut and showed it to me first,” Jack says. “Before she remembered she hates me.”

“She doesn’t hate you. She’s been hating you on my behalf since January.” Lena shakes her head against his coat. “It’s a lot of work. She’s exhausted. And this afternoon in the Marigny she danced with Kevin for half an hour straight so she wouldn’t have to look at us. Laney doesn’t dance with *Kevin*. Kevin can *dance*, it turns out, and she didn’t even look surprised.”

And once they start looking for it, it’s everywhere. Theo on the parade route handing his phone across a cooler to Kevin, screen down — *I can’t be trusted.* Laney at Endymion throwing a plush red heart the size of a pillow back into the crowd like it had the pin pulled — *NO hearts.* And back at the corner of the square, a girl with a coconut deciding all at once that every single one of them was faint.
“They’re eating Lucky Dogs,” Lena says. “Right now. Somewhere on Bourbon Street, Theo Vance and Laney Price are eating Lucky Dogs *on purpose*.”
“Margot too.”
“Margot’s being held against her will.” She looks off into the fog. “Margot’s been taking notes on us since August. She’ll say it was research.”
“It was research.”
“Kevin told them,” Jack says. “Under the dinosaurs at Cabazon. ‘Respectfully. Leave it alone.’ And in the van, when they started up again: ‘I said leave it alone. In January.’”
“In *January*.” Lena looks up at him through the wet. “Kevin Phạm is the only grown-up on this trip.”
Out on the river the ferry is a lit shape going under the fog, its last run. Neither bank is there anymore.
“We don’t tell them,” she says.
“Not a word.”
“Not till it’s true.” She looks out at the white where the water was. “Let them eat their hot dogs.”

choices.text: “We should send them a fruit basket.”
response: “We should send them a fruit basket.”
“We should send them a *bill*.” And she laughs into the fog with her head back, and the fog takes it and doesn’t give any of it back.

choices.text: “They threw the towel in, in Arizona. They picked it back up.”
response: “They threw the towel in, in Arizona,” he says. “They picked it back up.”
“They did,” she says, and the laugh gets out of her, surprised — a short bright sound over the water that she didn’t send and doesn’t take back. “They did. With a *coconut*.”

He laughs, and she hears him start and goes with him, and then they’re both gone — her laugh with all its sound in it, shaking, his under it — for longer than any of it deserves, on a wet step in the fog with the city going on without them. The fog takes it.
“Hot dogs,” she says, when she can. “On *purpose*.”

s12h.slug: TUESDAY · 11:12 PM · THE MOONWALK — NOT THE PICTURES
body: The laugh goes out of her slowly. By the time it’s gone the roar of the Quarter is coming through the white muffled, like a party in the next apartment.
She tips her face up to him. Her medal has come out of her collar on its chain, and she has it between her finger and thumb.
“Tell me about her,” she says. “Not the pictures. Her.”
It’s the one he’d skip, if she were letting him skip anything. She isn’t. And she ought to know what it is he’s putting down.

“She’s the funniest person I’ve ever met,” he says. “I don’t mean she tells jokes. She’ll do my mother, or Hale, or a waitress in Youngstown, before she’ll answer a question as herself, and she’s so good at it you forget you asked. And she’s the bravest person in any room she walks into. She walks in and everybody turns around, and she knows it before they do, and she walks in anyway.”

body.text: “She came to Mass with me. I didn’t ask her to. She sat there and watched everything like she was taking notes, and afterward she made me explain it properly, start to finish. The next time she knelt down next to me at St. Brendan’s.”
“She walked at the March for Life with me, in San Francisco. It cost her, and she knew exactly what it was going to cost before she got out of the car.”

“There was a fundraiser her people set up. She could have walked me through it like a coat she’d borrowed. Instead she took it apart for me — got every one of those people to say what they actually thought, and then she stood back and let me give them the real arguments instead of the cartoon.”

body: He hears his own voice going on and doesn’t stop it. “She didn’t want to win. She wanted to understand what I believe. I don’t know anybody else who ever wanted that who didn’t already believe it.”

body.text: “I told her something Father Osei would say. That there’s good between two people and there’s bad, and the bad doesn’t cancel the good. And she said, ‘Say the last part again.’ And then she said it wasn’t in the book, and I said, ‘It’s in him,’ and she was quiet a long time after that.”

body: “She told my brother how we met. Danny was on the phone, on his birthday, and she told him this whole made-up story about some trick I pulled to get her to go out with me, and he was dying, he couldn’t breathe — and then she stopped doing it and told him the truth. The window seat. What I said about the grandmother. A lie would’ve been funnier, and she knew it, and she told him the true one.”
“Was she kind to you?” Lena asks.
“Yes.”
“Good,” she says, and nothing on her face changes, and her eyes stay on his.

“She’s the one I can tell the truth to. I said that to my brother on the phone with her listening, and it was true when I said it.” The fog moves on the steps below them. “She wanted to be with me in the daylight. She was good at it.”

body.text: “You asked me in the van if I was happy. I said yes. It was true.”

body: “I thought about Christmas in Youngstown with her at my grandmother’s table. I had the chair picked out. I wanted to be the one who sent her the first thing, not the last.”

“I skipped a Saints game for her in January,” he says. “I told her why I was skipping it, and she said, ‘Teach me it.’ So I taught her it. She asked better questions than Remy.” The fog has her hair now, a fine wet on it. “She reads a book like she’s going to have to play every person in it. You can’t win an argument with her about a story. She’s already been all of them.”
He stops, and makes himself say the next part too, because it’s true and she asked for all of it. “I’m going to miss her. I already do.”
She doesn’t move. The medal stays where it is in her fingers, and it catches what light the lamp still has.
“I watched you answer her,” Lena says. “All week. Every call. In the kitchen with Mama at the stove, at a gas pump in Arizona, on a stoop on Royal Street this afternoon. You never let it ring once.”
“I wasn’t going to be that,” he says. “On top of all the rest.”
“I know you weren’t.” Her thumb moves once on the medal. “That’s how I knew it was real. A man doesn’t pick up on a stoop on Royal Street for a picture.”
There’s a word for it.

body.text: He has said it to Skye on the phone with Lena ten feet away.

body: “She’s —” he says.
“I know what the word is, Jack. Don’t you say it.”
He doesn’t.

“It was never the pictures,” she says. “All January I thought, if I ever had to hear it, it’d be the pictures that killed me. I *wanted* it to be the pictures. Some girl on the internet in a tank top — I could have hated a tank top. I’m good at hating a tank top. I was raised by Mémère.” Her eyes don’t leave his. They’re wet and they don’t go anywhere. “It was never the pictures. It was that it was real.”
She says the other half herself.
“And you’re giving that up.”
“Yes.”
“For —”
She doesn’t finish it. He doesn’t either. The fog has the lamp now, and the two of them under it, and the rest of the Moonwalk is gone.

s12i.slug: TUESDAY · 11:22 PM · THE MOONWALK — AN INDEX CARD
body: Lena hasn’t moved since she stopped on *For —*. She sits facing him inside the Carhartt between his knees, the tin a hard corner at her collarbone, her medal still in her fingers, and she looks hard at the third button of his shirt.
“The dinner,” she says at last. “I told you we’d get to the dinner.”
He waits.

“Julian is good.” She says it to the button first, and then she lifts her head and says it to him, because that seems to be the rule tonight. “He’s good, Jack. He’s the kindest man I know, and the most patient, and heaven knows I’ve tested it — I’ve tested that man like a seawall. He doesn’t believe one thing I believe. Not one. And some weeks he lives it better than I do. He’d hate me for saying that, so I never have. I’m saying it to you.”
“You know I was going to end it after Christmas,” she says. “I told you that.”
The band on Decatur has gone quiet. In the gap he can hear a woman somewhere on the square laughing at something, on and on.
“I didn’t tell you it was for you,” Lena says.
Nothing on the end of it. She puts it there between them and leaves it.

“I decided at home. On Mama’s back steps, in my coat, after we’d hung up one night — I don’t even know which night anymore, they all ran together into one long night with snow on your end. I’d sit out there after with the phone going cold in my hand and think, that’s the person I tell things to. And if that’s the person I tell things to, then I owe Julian a true thing. So I wrote it down. You know me. I don’t trust my face with anything I mean. An index card, in capitals, so my hand wouldn’t shake on it. For the dinner — his birthday dinner, the Monday after. After Hale. Two days late, because he’d been home for it.”
Another card. Of course it was a card. She looks off into the fog.

“I had it in my pocket at that seminar. All through Dido. I had it in my pocket while you sat at the other end of that table and didn’t look at me. And Sunday night I’d seen what I’d seen.” She doesn’t say what. She told him an hour ago: the status, the gate. “So Monday I sat across from him at a table with a candle on it, with that card in my coat, and I didn’t use it. I let him order for me. I let him take a picture.”
“I saw the picture.”
“I know you did,” she says. “That’s why I let him take it.”
He remembers it, in 412, on a Tuesday morning, on a screen: *birthday dinner, two days late*, and her name on it.
“Fury,” Lena says. “And pride. Two of the seven at one table, and I didn’t even get dessert.”
“I made a good man a guardrail, Jack. I did exactly what you did with Becca, and I called *you* names for it.”
He starts to say something. He doesn’t know yet what.
“And it’s not the same,” she says. “You know it’s not the same. I never —”
She stops. Her mouth stays open on the next word, and then it closes over it.
“Is it still —”
“In my wallet.” Her free hand goes back to the hip pocket of her jeans and lies flat over it and doesn’t take anything out. “It’s his. He reads it first.”
He will never know what it says. That seems right to him, and he’s surprised how right.
“Sunday,” she says. “After Mass. To his face, when we’re both back.” And then, to the fog: “Five weeks and a day. It’s been in my wallet five weeks and a day.”

One index card. One sentence on a phone, in his father’s garage, with the space heater ticking and the snow coming down past the window in the side door. Any night since Christmas. Any night before it.
“If I’d said it on the phone,” he says. “Any one of those nights.”
“If I had said what *fix it* meant.”
“If I’d said, I don’t have a thing, Lena. I’ll be by the phone.”
“If I had told you on the back steps instead of telling a card.”
“If I’d told you on the stairs at All Souls that I was waiting.”
“If I had asked you what for.”

They go on a little longer, quietly, and every one of them starts the same way. Nobody hands anybody a *you*. It’s like the line on the Broussards’ shed, four and a half feet up the boards, where you can see exactly how high it came, and know exactly how little it would have taken to keep it out, and not be able to make it not have come.

So he says it now, the thing he kept under the oak with her fingers coming loose from his button.
“Me too. Since the porch. Since before you told me your name.”
Her hand closes, slowly, over the medal.
Lena draws back far enough to see him.
“Plain, Jack,” she says. “From now on. Even when it’s ugly. *Especially* then.”
“Plain.”

“I know you do.” She looks at him from inside the coat, with the fog in her hair beading on every strand. “That’s what scares me about you.”

“Yes,” she says. “You should have. And I should have let you.”
Whatever it was, the end of it is still back in December, at the dash, with a van coming. He doesn’t reach for it now, and she doesn’t.
“Plain,” he says. “Like Ohio.”
“Ohio’s beige,” Lena says, into his collar. But her hand comes off the medal, and after a moment it pats his chest twice, like a woman testing whether a melon is ready.

s12j.slug: TUESDAY · 11:30 PM · THE MOONWALK, UNDER THE LAMP — THE TIN
body: The lamp at the head of the steps hangs in the fog with a pale wheel around it, and the light that comes down through the wheel is soft and wet and lands on her hair, and on his hands, and on the step between his boots.

He has to reach in under her chin for it. It’s been against her all night at the collarbone, a corner she found in the first minute at the rail and touched through the canvas and left alone. He works his hand into the breast pocket of the Carhartt, and she leans back to let him, and he brings it out warm from the two of them.
“You said if there was one more,” he says, “you’d know.”
He puts it in her hands.

Her thumbs know it before she looks at it. They go over the lid in the dark — the soft corners, the hinge, the letters — and stop on the first R, where his thumb has worn the paint down to bare tin from two months of riding on it. She looks at that a while.
“At the coffee cart,” she says. “With my finger on the lid. I said it to make you laugh.”
“I didn’t laugh.”
“No. You put it in your pocket like I’d handed you a finger bone of Saint Somebody in a glass box.”

“It went to Youngstown,” he says. “It sat on the workbench in my dad’s garage every night I called you, next to the space heater. It went to Christmas Mass. It came back on the plane. It rode across Texas in this pocket while you weren’t speaking to me.”
“Stop it.” Her thumb is on the lid. “I am not going to cry over an Altoids tin on a levee in front of Algiers.”
“Algiers is gone.”
“Then in front of the fog.”
She sets it on her knee, inside the coat, and he keeps his arm around her, and she opens it under the lamp.

The smell comes up first: sweet and stale and shut-in, Christmas in a pocket. Her eleven are there, packed tight, each on its slip in her capitals, and No. 1 on its curl of receipt paper from a soup restaurant in Buellton.

body.text: And on top of hers, fitted in close, six more. Six Reds, each on a strip of yellow paper torn along the blue lines, in a hand that isn’t hers: small and slanting and pressed hard into the paper, a hand no teacher ever got anywhere with.
She takes one out by its corner and tips it to the lamp.
*No. 13 · 1/20/10 · Delgado east stairwell, 3:40 a.m. · after the Fishbowl*
She puts it back on its Red exactly where it was and takes out another.
*No. 15 · 1/27/10 · Hale’s deck, 7:37 p.m. · after Hale’s*
That one she holds longer. She puts No. 15 back and takes out the last one, the one on top.
*No. 17 · 2/5/10 · El Paso, under the air pump, 11:55 p.m. · after the drive*
“El Paso,” she says. “Where was I?”
“In the van. Asleep.”
“I wasn’t asleep.”

He can see the van at the pump: the dome light off, her shape against the far window with her face turned to the glass. He’d stood under the air pump with his back to it so he wouldn’t have to find out whether she was watching.

The rest she reads where they lie, tipping the tin to the light, and her lips move on them as they move at the back of Holy Rosary on a decade when she thinks she’s alone: the number, the date, the place, what it came after. He watches her read the stairwell, and Sully’s, and the curb. He watches her get to the drive.
There’s nothing on top of them. He had nothing to put in. She lifts the slips with one fingernail and looks under them anyway, all the way to the bottom of the tin.
“When did you write these?”
“Last night. In the attic, by the streetlight.” He tips his head at the yellow. “Off the bottom of Hale’s pad.”
“You tore up Hale’s essay for me.”
“I tore off the bottom. The essay’s at the top.”
“There’s one sentence at the top, Jack.”
“It’s a good sentence.”
“It *is* a good sentence.” She says it to the tin, not to him, and for a little while she doesn’t say anything else, and the fog comes and goes around the lamp.

body.else: She looks up at him from the tin, and down at her eleven, by themselves.

body.text: She runs a fingernail down the yellow strips, down the ends of them, where the last words are. “Sully’s. The Fishbowl. The curb. Hale’s. *The Dead.* The drive.” She reads them off in order. “There isn’t one in here that’s her.”
“No.”
“Not one.”
“With her I never wanted one.”
Lena takes that in with her eyes on the tin. “So I’m the near occasion of sin and she’s the cure. I don’t know whether to light a candle or file a grievance.”
“Both.”
“Both,” she agrees, to the lid.

She takes her own No. 1 out on its curl of receipt paper — the Lighthouse, the first night, before he knew there was any such thing as a tin — and lays it on her knee beside his No. 17, August next to February, and looks at the two of them together under the lamp. Then she puts them back where they go, hers at the bottom, his on top.

body: In half an hour it’s Lent, and he’s done with them, all forty days of it; and whatever gets counted after tonight is going to get counted knowing exactly what it’s for.
Lena puts her hand over the open tin, the way you’d cover a cup at a table so nobody fills it.
“It’s mine,” she says.

“I know,” she says. “I can read.”
But she doesn’t sound like she’s won anything. She puts the strips straight with one finger, every edge, and closes the lid down on them with both thumbs till it catches.

She waits for them, so he tells her the four. The Hollis back steps, the Monday of Dido, with the pack open in his hand. The Delgado front steps two days after that. The east stairwell at the end of January, the same stairwell as No. 13, the other way round. The far end of the Anacapa lot the night before the drive, in the dark past the last light, with the Odyssey sitting there packed.
She listens to all four with her hand on the lid.
“Then that’s four I’d have taken off you,” she says, and shuts it.

“I *would* have known.” She snaps the lid shut on it with one thumb, a sound like a latch. “I’d have known in January. I’d have smelled it on you across a seminar table, Costigan, I just wasn’t speaking to you.”

s12k.slug: TUESDAY · 11:38 PM · THE MOONWALK — NOBODY’S OTHER ANYTHING
body: She puts the tin in the chest pocket of her jean jacket, the one that’s too small for anything, and it goes in, just, and she buttons the flap down over it.

His legs have turned to wood on the step. They get up without letting go of each other, and it is worse than getting down was: she stands first, still inside the coat, and pulls, and he comes up off the wet boards with his knees cracking like Tony’s, and she says “Saint Joseph and all the carpenters,” to his knees. Then they’re standing at the top of the steps under the lamp, as they stood at the rail two hours ago, her inside his open Carhartt, facing him, the fog coming up the steps behind her, her palms on his chest.

Down on Decatur the crowd has turned and is moving the other way now, up toward Bourbon, toward the horses: feathers and garbage-bag capes and a man carrying a cardboard pirogue over his head, a girl in a tiara on somebody’s shoulders with a go-cup in each hand. Somebody is blowing a whistle in the rhythm of the Who Dat. It’s twenty minutes to Lent, and the city knows it.
“So,” she says.
“So.”

“I’m not starting this as anybody’s other anything.” She says it to his face, every word. “Not yours, not hers, not his. I spent two months being somebody’s girlfriend while I was out on my mama’s back steps being — whatever I was on those steps. I won’t do that to anybody again. I won’t do it to *you*.”
“Me neither,” he says. “I’ve had a phone ringing in this pocket and your tin in the same pocket since Christmas. Nobody’s other anything.”

“Sunday. I told you. After Mass. To his face, when we’re both back. The card, and whatever he wants to say to me after it, and he’s allowed all of it. He’s going to be kind about it. That’s what I can’t stand. He’s going to be kind to me about it, and I’m going to have to sit there and let him.”
“Tuesday,” he says. “When she’s back from Vancouver.”

He tries to see Tuesday and can’t. All he can see is her listening — the way she listens when it’s real, all of her turned toward it like a plant toward a window — and him having to keep on talking into that.

body.text: “I promised her. To her face.”
body.else: “To her face. That’s the least of it.”

body: “Tell her everything.”
“I’m going to.”
“Tell her about tonight. Tell her nothing happened.”
“Nothing did.”
“Tell her anyway,” Lena says. “I would want it said.”
“She ought to get it from somebody who isn’t standing on a levee with you inside his coat.”
“Then I’d better get out of your coat,” Lena says, and doesn’t. “By Tuesday night.”
“By Tuesday night.”
“And till then, nothing. Nothing either one of us would have to explain. Not to them. Not to Mama. Not in a confessional.”
“Nothing.”
“And you don’t kiss me.”
“I know.”
“I’m not telling you,” she says. “I’m telling me.”
“Augustine tried that. He told himself *not yet* for about ten years.”
“Augustine wasn’t going to be a lawyer. I practice on myself.”
“Then stop looking at my mouth.”
“I’m not.”
“You are. You have been since the rail.”
“So have you. I’m allowed,” Lena says. “I’m from here.” But her eyes come up off his mouth to his eyes, which is harder.
What comes after Tuesday doesn’t get said. There’ll be a Wednesday; that’s as far as he can see from the top of these steps, and it’s far enough.
“What are you giving up?” she says. “For Lent.”
“Cigarettes.”
“…I know.” Her hand comes off his chest and goes to the flap of her pocket, over the tin, and rests there.
“You?”
“Something Laney’s going to take personally.”
“Coffee?”
“I’m giving something up, Jack. I’m not *dying*.”
She doesn’t say anything. He doesn’t. The band on Decatur goes into something slow. Her hand comes back to his chest. The fog goes on climbing the steps.
She takes her hands off his chest.

It happens slowly enough that he feels every part of it: the heel of each hand, then the palms, then the fingertips last, and where they were the cold comes straight in through the flannel. She steps back out of his coat. One step. The Carhartt comes off her shoulders and swings back against his own, empty, and all the warm that has been in it for two hours goes out the front of him at once, into the fog, the way heat goes out of a kitchen when somebody opens the back door in January. The tin goes with her, in her pocket, the hard corner of it gone from his chest. And she takes another step.

His coat hangs open on nothing. His arms are still a little out from his sides, the shape of her. He wants her back inside it so badly it’s like a hand on the back of his neck, pushing. He doesn’t move. *Hail Mary,* he thinks, *full of grace,* and gets no further than that, and it’s enough to keep his boots where they are on the wet boards.
“Pulling away,” she says, flat. “Watch me do it.”

He watches her do it. She doesn’t go anywhere. She stands two steps off at the top of the levee with her arms crossed tight over the pocket with the tin in it, shaking a little, and she waits for him.

She watches it go every inch of the way.
When he gets to the top she uncrosses her arms, and they go down off the Moonwalk together, side by side, toward the white cathedral and the roaring.

She turns toward the steps down to Decatur, and he comes up level with her.

Something happens at the corner of her mouth that she puts away again. “Then walk me to it, Youngstown.”

s13.slug: TUESDAY · 11:52 PM · BOURBON STREET AT ST. ANN — THE HORSES
body: They walk up St. Ann from the square, past the dark mule stalls and the shut shops on Chartres and the lit galleries on Royal, side by side, a hand’s width apart, on purpose. Every block it gets louder. Every block he could close it, and every block he doesn’t, and she doesn’t, and the not-closing it is the hardest walking he has ever done.

Bourbon Street at eight minutes to midnight is the last of everything at once. It’s packed curb to curb and lit pink and green and gold from the bars, and the asphalt is shining wet with every kind of liquid and paved with beads, a crust of them, cracking underfoot. Up on a balcony a speaker is playing “TiK ToK” down at the street at full volume, and the people on the balcony are throwing the last of everything they have down into the crowd: beads, a stuffed alligator, a shoe. A man in a Superman cape and a Saints helmet is being walked home between two friends, his feet still going and the rest of him not.

The others are on the corner where Luc told them to be. Theo and Laney each have a Lucky Dog in its paper, a bite out of each, going cold. Laney has the coconut held against her chest with her other arm, high up, like a heart she’s afraid she’ll drop. Margot is beside her with her hands in her coat. Kevin has his in his windbreaker, the right one around Theo’s phone. And Remy, found, somehow, in a purple Afro wig he can’t account for, is telling Margot about Frenchmen Street in a voice that suggests Frenchmen Street did something to him.

Laney sees them first. She reads Lena’s face, and then Jack’s, and gets nothing off either, and her mouth opens and shuts. Theo has gone very still. He looks at Jack about as long as it takes to read a page, and gets nothing either, and then he looks away down Bourbon at the lights.
“We got y’all a Lucky Dog,” Laney says, holding hers out.
“Nobody wants a Lucky Dog, Laney,” says Lena, and takes the place on the curb next to her, and Jack takes the place next to Lena.
Then the street changes.

It starts the way Luc said it would. First a pressure in the crowd up the block, toward Canal, before there’s anything to see, a whistle and the bars’ music cut off one door at a time and people turning to look. And then over the heads, high up, the horses: mounted police, forming a line across Bourbon from one curb to the other, and then coming down the street at a walk. They’re huge up close. They blow white into the cold, and their shoes ring on the wet asphalt through the beads, and the riders sit up there in the dark blue and say nothing to anybody. They don’t need to. The crowd goes ahead of them, slowly, unhurried and complaining, like water ahead of a broom. Somebody near the corner yells “Mardi Gras is *over*!” and half the street cheers and the other half boos, and the balcony speaker cuts off in the middle of the chorus.

Behind the horses come the trucks: the street sweepers with their round brushes going, and behind them the water trucks, wetting it all down, beads and cups and the shoe, washing Mardi Gras into the gutters in one long gray roll. The smell of it comes ahead of them, wet pavement and diesel and soap.

On foot behind the horses, in the line, in the dark blue with his cap square on his head, is Luc. He sees his sister on the curb. He takes two fingers off his belt, and that’s hello. And then he sees who she’s standing next to, and how, and he looks at that for the length of three steps, and nothing on his face moves at all, and he walks on behind the horses.
“Ritual closure,” Margot says, watching the line go by. “Enforced by livestock.”
Kevin takes his right hand out of his windbreaker. Theo is looking at his own watch, and the second hand is coming up on the twelve. Kevin holds the phone out to him.
“Lent,” Kevin says.
Theo takes it. “What do I give up?”
“You already did.”
Theo turns the phone on. It lights in his hand, an apple on a black field, and he holds it, and doesn’t look at it.
Somewhere toward the river a bell starts, and Jack loses count of it under the trucks.

The horses go on down Bourbon toward the Marigny end, and the brushes after them, and the water trucks after the brushes, and where they’ve been the street is suddenly a street: black and wet and shining under the bar lights, a few beads in the gutter the brushes missed, people going home in costumes they look embarrassed by now. A man picks up his shoe. Lena stands beside Jack on the curb, not touching him, close enough that he can feel the cold she’s keeping. It’s Lent.

s13a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:08 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE AT DECATUR
body: They walk out of the Quarter, the seven of them strung out along the sidewalk, not saying much, with the trucks grinding away behind them on Bourbon. Remy goes out front jingling his mother’s keys over his head like a sleigh bell. Laney carries the coconut in both arms. Margot walks beside her with her collar up. Kevin walks with his hands in his empty pockets, and Theo beside him carries his phone, still lit, still not looked at. At Esplanade the Mint stands lit at the river end, and the oaks start, reaching over the avenue from both sides with beads up in them, purple and green and gold, years of them, a strand stirring now and then when the air does.
Lena walks on the inside, by the iron fences, with her hands in her pockets and one of them over the flap with the tin under it.
The RAZR goes off in the breast pocket of the Carhartt, alone in there now, against the place the tin was.

s13b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:12 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE, UNDER THE OAKS
body: He shuts the phone and puts it back over his heart.

Lena starts walking again, and he catches her up in four steps and falls in beside her. The oaks go over them, block after block, with the old beads hanging in the branches, and a streetlight, and dark, and a streetlight. Behind them, toward the river, the trucks are still at it, a long way off now, and the city is quieter than he has ever heard it, and it’s Wednesday.

Two miles up the avenue, past Broad, on Dupre Street, Celeste will have left the porch light on. Jack and Lena walk to the car under the oaks, not touching, not hurrying, carrying the space between them the whole way like something full to the brim.
